speech, but I just ask you to ask the memb er, once you have ruled, not to comment on
your ruling, as he just did.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is breaking up his speech. It does not help the
good order of the House.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I will refrain from commenting in
response to that. Here is a member who wa s in the House yester day crying crocodile
tears over the closure of schools in Christ church, when he closed more schools in
Taranaki with one stroke of a pen than any other member in this House, and there was
no justification for that. So that member knows no different. He has always been the
same. That is about where I will leave that.
Going back to the issue of  climate change and the environmental effects brought
about by our primary sector, it would be so he lpful to this debate and so helpful to the
economy of New Zealand if, at some stage,  a few facts were introduced into the
19 Sep 2012 General Debate 5385
discussion. So far, there has been a range of events in this discussion that have not been
able to substantiate those facts.
If we do accept—and I do not—that 50 perc ent of the greenhouse gas from New
Zealand comes from agriculture—and it certainly is challengeable in science—then
what would introducing a tax on that achieve in terms of climate change? What would it
achieve? What it would do is drive production from one of the most efficient production
systems offshore. Therefore, you would have  those levels of production being produced
in countries that have higher greenhouse ga s emissions from their production systems,
and less production in New Z ealand. Explain to me how that would help the New
Zealand economy, given the dependence of  the New Zealand economy on agricultural
exports.
It is without the slightest bit of rational e or logic that we would introduce a tax on
greenhouse gas emissions from our agricultura l sector. Those who pr omote that clearly
have no interest in watching “New Zealand Inc.” improve or grow, and have no interest
in improving the standard of living of New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: Women’s Suffrage Day
celebrates women’s right to vot e. As we have heard a nu mber of speakers say, New
Zealand was the first country in the world to al low that to occur. This is a day that we
should be able to celebrate. This is a day wh ere we should all be able to join together
and celebrate the wonderfulness of having been that first country that acknowledged the
role of women in our country’s democracy.
I think the other place that we should be r eally thinking of today is Christchurch,
because, of course, Christchurch was home to Kate Sheppard and those other suffragists
who really led the way. We memorialised  them in a wonderful memorial in
Christchurch, which, unfortunately, is not in a location that we can access, due to the
earthquakes.
But not everyone in Christchur ch is actually feeling like  celebrating today, because
democracy is something that has been challenged. People are feeling demoralised.
People are feeling powerless to act in the fa ce of what they see as an erosion of
democracy. When we look at what has happened in Christchurch—our city, our schools,
and our environment—all of the democratic institutions around those three
fundamentals of where I come from have all been challenged. The democratic voice of
the people has been stilled by the Government.
I want to remind the House that democracy is  more than the right to vote. It means a
lot more than that. Sure, we have the expression of democracy—representative
democracy—when we cast our vote, and we co me to this place to represent those who
send us here. But it is about guaranteeing basi c human rights. It is about the separation
of powers, it is about freedom of expressi on, and it is about good governance. That is
what a democratic country looks like.
I am afraid that every single one of those features of a democracy that I have spoken
of has been threatened in Christchurch today.  These were all things that the suffragists
actually stood for when they petitioned Parliament for the right to vote. I want to remind
the House that nearly a quarter of all adult voting-age women in this country signed that
petition at that time. It was extraordin ary. Over 30,000 women signed the petition for
the right to vote. What we are challenging th e Government to do today is to trust the
people. Go back those 119 years to when this  Parliament trusted the people. It trusted
every single one of its citizen s of voting age with the right to vote. Let us see that we
can trust the people today as we, hopefully, restore democracy to Environment
Canterbury, restore democracy to the Christchurch City Council, and restore democracy
to our schools.
5386 General Debate 19 Sep 2012
At 5.30 p.m. tonight at the Bri dge of Remembrance in Christchurch there will be a
gathering where there will be a new rebuild ing suffrage petition launched. That petition
is designed to restore democracy to our cit y, to our schools, and to our environment.
The purpose of the petition is to renew the gr eat democratic legacy of Christchurch for
our children. That is whom the petition aims to support. Vote Canterbury Kids speaks to
our proud history of universal  suffrage in New Zealand, it speaks to the loss of
democracy that we have suffered in Christchurch today, and it speaks to the future for
our children. That is what the petition is all about.
It is wonderful that Christchurch sees th e launch of this modern suffrage petition,
with its call for democracy. I want the Government to listen to the people. Many
Christchurch residents are hu rting. They are bewildered. They are struck by bombshell
announcements around their land, their homes , the Earthquake Commission, insurance,
and, now, school closures. Nobody is saying that these are no t hard decisions, but they
are impacting on people through the way they are being presented to them as final
decisions, with the people not being empowered to have a say about their future.
At the school meeting I attended the other night one pers on said that the
announcement had done what 10,000 aftershocks had not done. If that school closes, his
family leaves. I do not want anyone to leave Christchurch because they have not had a
say in rebuilding its future.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: It is a great pleasure to ri se to speak in this general
debate. I join my female colleagues across the House in congratulating all women and
celebrating the 119th Women’s Suffrage Day. I remember  the centenary celebrations in
Auckland. That was probably the first time I had actually heard about the suffragettes,
because, as a migrant, I had heard that New Zealand had in fact given the vote to
women first around the world, but I had not actually heard the stories about Kate
Sheppard. So I feel very proud to be a New Zealander. But, having  said that, I would
like to comment on a couple of things that were actually said before by Sue Moroney.
Miss Moroney talked about how Kate Sheppard would be ashamed of our stance on
the extended paid parental leave that Labour  proposed. I have to say that in my view
Kate Sheppard would be ashamed of Miss Moroney. She stood for ambition. She stood
for equality. I do not know, but back in t hose days, I would have thought that the
suffragettes would have actually carried thei r babies, fighting for equal rights, on their
backs or on their fronts. They would not ha ve actually sat there and said that they
wanted 6 months’ paid parental leave. I ha ve to say, as a mum who actually went back
to work, who actually took res ponsibility for my own chil d, I actually went back to
work and I should not be made to feel emba rrassed or ashamed that I went to work and
that I was not a good mother, which is what the Opposition tries to make us feel.
We are proud parents. We are proud mother s. We are women. Do not say in this
House that Kate Sheppard would be ashame d of us. I think she would be ashamed of
Sue Moroney for saying that women should cower and say “We are women. We should
have more. We actually deserve more than th is.” I do not think so. Kate Sheppard stood
for equality. She stood for ambition and aspi ration for women. That is not what she
actually asked for.
Annette King was talking about homelessn ess and single women. Of course, none of
us celebrate that. We all want to make su re that all New Zealanders, including women,
have better opportunities and do not have issues with homele ssness. But I have to say I
am surprised that she commented on that , because the Labour Opposition has opposed
every single initiative that  this Government has proposed to improve the lot for New
Zealanders, including things like more mining for oil and gas exploration. What about
making welfare work? The Opposition oppos ed a 90-day probation period for new
employees. It actually opposed that. Thirteen thousand new jobs were created as a result
19 Sep 2012 General Debate 5387
of that particular policy, and 60 percent of the employers would not have gone out there
and given that new person a j ob had it not been for that particular policy. Thirteen
thousand new jobs is a lot of new jobs.
Foreign investment is another initiative the Opposition actually opposed. What about
foreign investment? Let us talk about Mr Cameron, the Canadian film maker. James
Cameron moved and bought a farm, a big, big, big farm, in the Wairarapa. He invested
millions and millions of dollars in the Wairarapa. The Opposition opposes foreign
ownership. Let me say, Mr Cameron just an nounced, I think, that he is going to be
making a sequel to Avatar, which will create 1,500 new jobs. Hobbit haters, Avatar
haters, I say let us actually celebrate th ese kinds of investments. They provide
investment in New Zealand, and they provi de more opportunities and more jobs for
New Zealanders.
What about the public sector reform? What about the health service? I have to say
that I love the fact that we have more doctors, we have mo re nurses, and we have more
midwives remaining in New Zealand inst ead of going overseas, because we have
created an opportunity for them to stay here. The bonding scheme has meant that we
have, in total, 1,800 more nurses—1,800—263 more doctors, 218 more midwives, and
13 more radiation therapists who have stay ed in New Zealand since that scheme was
introduced in 2009. I remember back in—

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I join my colleagues in rising to speak
to Women’s Suffrage Day and the status of  women in our country at the moment, 119
years on from achieving universal suffrage in this country. Just a quick note: I am
surprised that none of the men have spoken in this debate on the benefits of having our
voices in Parliament.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I wanted to.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Thank you, Grant. I join my Labour colleagues, very strangely, in
wondering what Kate Sheppard and Meri  Mangakahia would be thinking of our
democracy and our society today. I do not ne ed to have a séance to know that they
would be expecting more from this country and more from this Government, because I
expect more, and I do not think even I am as radical as they were back in their day.
They were some pretty fierce women. Th ey were obviously fans of democracy and
women’s involvement in decision making. To  quote Kate Sheppard, one of her goals
was that “All that separates, whether of race,  class, creed, or sex, is inhuman, and must
be overcome.” In particular, she was concer ned about establishing legal and economic
independence of women from men. She was not wholly occupied with advancing
women’s rights, however, but also found time to promote pol itical reforms such as
proportional representation and the wider movement for democracy.
Meri requested not only that M āori women be given the vote back at that time, but
that they be eligible to sit in the M āori Parliament, thus going a step further even than
her P ākehā contemporaries of the European suffrage movement. Although I do not
believe that it is my place to comment on the processes of tino rangatiratanga, I would
like to point out that whom the Crown choos es to consult with and how it consults
makes a difference. I really doubt that Meri Mangakahia would approve of the proposed
process of consultation around asse t sales. This is not consulta tion; it is tokenism. That
is not too dissimilar from the reality of the time when she was speaking out, when
women could speak but they could not be hear d. I also think she w ould be pretty angry
that over 120 years after sh e spoke out to affirm M āori women’s leadership, M āori
women’s leadership has been eroded by systematic issues such as violence and
gendered poverty.
To speak more to Kate’s issues, I note again, with my colleague Lianne Dalziel, that
Kate was a proud Cantabrian and a fighter fo r wider democracy. So today to see that
5388 General Debate 19 Sep 2012
loss of democracy in her place of birth and her site of struggle is  a particularly sad
thing, and not a reason for celebration. As we see the closure of schools and mergers
that threaten to take away the heart of so many communities, we know what she would
be saying. When we see the powers of th e city council being taken over by the
unelected Government body of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority, with no
plan in sight for how this power will be returned, we know she would not be happy. We
may not all have always agreed with th e council in Christchur ch, but to rebuild
Christchurch without democracy threatens to  rebuild structures but not communities,
and Kate would not approve.
Today I went to the Women’s Suffrage Da y breakfast and heard the Minister of
Women’s Affairs speaking about  the status of women. Sh e noted that New Zealand
continues to be well regarded internationally  for our gender equality. Well, that may be
true, except for, you know, the 50-plus points that the United Nations Committee on the
Elimination of Discrimination Against Women suggested that our State needed to work
on. The Minister did acknowledge that we sti ll need to work towards greater economic
independence, improved safety from violence, and increased representation in all levels
and types of leadership for our women, but thinks the Government has committed to
doing its part.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): It is probably a bad start on Women’s
Suffrage Day that I have interrupted one of my female colleagues, Jan Logie, in her
speech, but there is process. Can I acknow ledge 119 years since women received the
vote in this country. I think it is important to begin, joining with my colleague Judith
Collins, who spoke at the start, by acknow ledging important New Zealand women and
their contribution, and in doing so to acknowledge our head of State, the Queen of New
Zealand, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth, for her 60 years of service, all of those women
who sit on the executive—my colleagues w ho are in Cabinet—those across the House
who sit here in Parliament from all partie s, those women who lead in the judiciary,
those who are in the Civil Se rvice, and, of course, those women who are our mothers,
our friends, and so forth, and the contribu tion they bring. When it comes to women’s
voting, my mother has always proudly voted, and certainly now with me in Parliament
she is never shy of an opinion to be shared, and she never hesitates there.
I want to turn to some of those who ha ve spoken in the House about what Kate
Sheppard and others would thi nk. I always think it is  an injustice to th eir voices to add
our presumption to them. I just want to repeat  that for the sake of those listening: when
we try to add our voices pres umptuously to what Kate Shep pard and others did, we do
them an injustice. We do not know what Kate  Sheppard would think about what we do
today, and I think there is a certain arrogance in doing that.
But as we turn to the modern day, I think it  is really great as a Kiwi and as a Kiwi
bloke to stand here to acknowle dge all that women are doing in  our society. I think it is
the women, certainly within the National caucus and the body as  a whole, who are
getting on with the business of getting thin gs done. We need only look this week at
some of the great announcements that have been put forward, including within welfare
and within education. We have had some also within the conservation area, and so forth.
Some really great initiatives are being led by women in this National caucus.
We are busy with getting on with the job. We are busy as a National caucus and a
National Government with getting on with th e job. I found in recent  days sitting on the
Education and Science Committee that we have been looking at the element of digital
literacy. How do we encourage young girls and boys  to learn to be the future of this
country? We have had some amazing examples  of men and women who are working to
enhance the digital understanding of our young people, and I mention this because there
is a great initiative happening within the electorate of T āmaki known as the
19 Sep 2012 General Debate 5389
Manaiakalani project, led by Russell Burt and the great team at  Pt England Primary
School. They are getting on with the job, and they are getting on with the job on their
own initiative but also with that wider suppo rt of a Government th at understands that
you empower individuals to be the best that  they can be. And I may be presumptuous,
therefore, to suggest that th at was the spirit of the suffragettes—to empower people to
be the best that they can be, operating within this New Zealand democracy.
I want to acknowledge too people such as  Desley Simpson, Kit Parkinson, Colin
Davis, and Mark Thomas of the local board in Ōrākei, also within my electorate of
Tāmaki. They are getting on with the job, be it  our local sports fields so that boys and
girls, men and women, can get out and about, or making sure places like T āmaki Drive
are open and accessible for all New Zealanders  to enjoy and to celebrate. These are
Kiwis working hard. They are men and wo men in our community working hard and
getting on with the job. And it is the National Government  that is standing there in
support, as well, so that the job gets done for the benefit of all New Zealanders.
I turn finally towards our business. I have been meeting with the business association
managers across my electorate : Sally in Ellerslie, Wendy in  St Heliers, and Gary down
in Glen Innes. Again, these are people suppo rting Kiwi businesses to get on with the
job, as new businesses are openi ng and there are opportunities. It has been the National
Government that stood behind them in many ways. We have talked  about the 90-day
trial period that we have put out, creat ing more than 13,000 jobs. We reduced the
business tax to 28c in the dollar, absolutely  supporting Kiwis to get on with the job. We
reduced ACC levies. In fact, th at was Minister Judith Collins, one of the fine women of
this House. New Zealanders are getting on with the job. We have had great
opportunities, and if I draw it, certainly, from the people of T āmaki, and those whom I
have mentioned, they are getting on with the job. They are getting on with the job with
the support of this Government, which is absolutely committed.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
HUTT CITY COUNCIL (GRAFFITI REMOVAL) BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I move, That the Hutt City
Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill be now read a third time . Very early in this debate I am
feeling a little bit of confusion, because th e run sheet I have says that the Minister
speaks here. I just wanted to know whether or not there has been an event, an invitation
from Mr Key, or an election, or  what the story is, but I will  assume, in fact, that the
member in charge of the bill should appropriately speak now.
This is a bill that is a relatively simple l ittle bill, one from the Hutt City Council, one
that is the brainchild of Ray Wallace, the Mayor of Hutt City. He is a very good mayor
of the independent city.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: That’s right—republic.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, I would not say we were a republic, but it is an
area that is proud of its i ndependence. Ray Wallace, when running for mayor, made
graffiti an important issue as part of his campa ign, and as part of that exercise we went
through some of the things that could be done to  reduce graffiti in Hutt City. It is fair to
say there has been a considerable amount of progress. I think Dave O’Sullivan’s team—
anyone who has any knowledge of rugby le ague history in New Zealand will know
former Detective Sergeant O’Sullivan, who is  a pretty mean second rower. I think he
was part of the Wainuiōmata champions team in the early 1990s. He has taken charge of
the contracting for removing graffiti, and he and his team work very, very well. They
work quickly. The Hutt City works on the basis that when this rubbish is up, it is better
5390 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
to get it down as soon as possible. It is taken down from places that can be viewed from
public places, especially from roads, wh ere it is on council land. There is an
arrangement with Telecom, the New Z ealand Railways Corporation, the power
companies, and a number of others to get rid of the stuff immediately, and, as a result of
that, the place looks a lot better.
They also do private property. The council wo rks on the basis that if it has an expert
team and it is going around the city every day anyway, it is better to use that team and
its expertise with paint and matching to pain t private property with the consent of the
property owners. The vast majority of prope rty owners are rapt. Some people tell me
that they did not even know th at they had graffiti on the fe nce, and they get a knock on
the door from the contractors from the council o ffering to paint it out. I think that it is a
damn good service, and it is something that we are proud of in the Hutt.
But, unfortunately, there are a few people who come, really, into two categories.
First, there are the owners of abandoned buildings. These are people who are often
offshore, have not got tenants in the build ings, or, very occasionally, have dubious
people who are in those buildings. It is hard to get a response as to whether or not the
graffiti should be painted out; to date it is always done with consent.
The effect of this bill is to  give the council ri ghts so that after an appropriate period
of notice in writing has been issued—about 10 working days’ notice; it is a couple of
weeks, effectively, although these people do work more than 5 days a week—if there
has not been a negative response from the landowner, it means that the council or its
contractors will be able to go on to the prope rty and get rid of the graffiti. That seems
like a logical thing to do.
There is a doubt about the pe riod. I think that these days  there is email and other
electronic contacts, and that is the way that most contact occurs. Out in the Hutt now,
most people pay their rates—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: You’ve got email in the Hutt?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: We have got lots of w onderful males in the Hutt,
including email, Mr Robertson. There is a question with an email delivery method of
whether in fact that might be better and th e period might be shorte r, but the view was
that because this law is new, and steps into an area that previously councils around New
Zealand have not, it was better to be a bit c onservative in bringing it in as to notice
periods. But I do want to make the point that  there is a point of balance, because the
effect of that is that you do leave graffiti up for longer than would otherwise be the case,
which slightly defeats the purpose.
There is quite a strong view in the Hutt th at the presence of graffiti, or tagging,
signals a lack of social cohesion. It does sometimes give a perception, generally an
unfair perception, of danger, and there is no doubt that it has an effect on property
values for the properties that are around the abandoned properties. Therefore, our view
is that it has a detrimental effect on our city, on the image, a nd on the well-being—the
feeling of well-being—of people. That is why we want to get rid of it.
The Summary Offences Act does provide le gal grounds to deter o ffenders and to do
some graffiti control. However, often the people who do this are, frankly, sneaky little
bastards who—sorry? Well, they  quite often are, Mr Spea ker. They are people who
sneak in, do the graffiti, and sneak away, and too often they are not caught in a way that
they can be prosecuted. What is also not avai lable under the Act is the ability, as I have
indicated, to go on to private property or ot her property that is visible from a public
place and clean it off without consent.
The package of measures—I want to say that some of them are negative. The
painting out, the decision to prosecute pe ople when caught defacing public property—
those are negative. But there is a lot of positive stuff that goes on with youth in the Hutt.
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5391
There is an attempt to divert. People like Councillor Ken Laban are doing a wonderful
job in the sports area, because there is a view that the kid in sport is not in court. That
sort of activity is very positive. Although the form of art is not one that I naturally warm
to, it is often the case that ma ny of these young people are, in fact, talented artists. If
they can be channelled towards murals and other things, then very  positive things can
happen.
I think anyone who has visi ted what we call the old village, what people call
Homedale, in Wainuiōmata, the village on the way down to the Rimutaka Forest Park—
it is a beautiful park; people should visit it—going through that village, will know there
is a wonderful mural of Tana Umaga and Pi ri Weepu. I think that has been up now for
maybe 5, 6, or 7 years. I tell you what, that does not get vandalised. No one—no one—
touches that mural, because th ere is community ownership. In  fact, some of the people
who painted it, and who might pr operly have been described as the little bastards of the
time, have now grown up and they are quite big. I think any suggestion that that mural
would be attacked—in fact, it would not happen.
I want to congratulate the Mayor of Hutt C ity, Ray Wallace, on his war on graffiti. I
want to thank the Local Government and Environment Committee for the very good
work that it did on the Hutt City Council (Graffi ti Removal) Bill. I think the changes it
made were an improvement to the bill. I want  to thank the chair of the select committee
for the way that she chaired it—in a way th at I am sure a number of her colleagues
could have lessons from to improve their abilities. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am absolutely delighted
to support this Hutt City Council (Graffiti Re moval) Bill at its third reading. I was
interested that Trevor Mallard said that it is a simple bill, and he is absolutely right. It is
simple, it is good, it is sensible, and it is strai ghtforward. I think it is a credit to the Hutt
City Council for bringing it to Parliament. We did not have to do much work on it at all,
just a few slight amendments and a few tweaks.
The Local Government and Environment Committee worked well on the bill. It was
actually interesting because a lot of these issu es of graffiti are th ings that we come
across in our own cities. Really, what this bill is all about, as Trevor Mallard has
explained, is giving the Hutt City Council the ability to enter private land to remove
graffiti from buildings that are in the public view—not around the back, but in the
public view—where it does have a bad influence on the community.
I am also interested in picking up on th e discussions about how  people feel about
graffiti in their community. The first thought about that—and I have had graffiti on my
house, because I live in the centre of Ch ristchurch; the house is now knocked down, but
before it was knocked down—is that it absolutely impinges on you. You wonder why
these people are painting nasty things all over your wall.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: It’s invasive.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: It is an invasion of your privac y. It is an invasion of something
that you care about, something that you have wo rked hard to look after, and something
that you have spent good money on too.
Graffiti is a major problem in the urban areas, and I have to say that the Hutt Valley
has been particularly hard hit with this. It is that damage to prope rty that upsets people.
It gives a symbol of neglect and it is some thing that the community really does want to
get rid of. The Hutt City Counc il does have good pr ocesses to deal with the problem. It
has actually invested significant amounts of m oney to remove graff iti. It has a rapid
removal process, and I believe that it  has very good contra ctors who are very
experienced in this  area, but it is not cheap. The council spends over $300,000 doing
that work. We support it because it is doing it for the good of the community.
5392 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
The problem that we are trying to address with this bill is the fact that some
landlords—not all, but some landlords, part icularly absentee landlords—do not respond
to the council when it requests the access to clean up their properties, and so the council
is stuck. It does not know how to deal with that. This bill will solve that problem.
We did get seven submissions  on the bill, and the major ity supported the bill, but
there were a few issues raised. One of the issu es that we dealt with, and we were really
quite careful about, was how we can clarify the difference between graffiti and art. This
is quite an interesting case, because how do you decide? Actually, in the end we chose a
definition that was consistent with section 11A of the Summary Offences Act 1981.
What this does is it identifies graffiti as something that damages and defaces. It actually
lists numerous methods you could use to do that, but the crucial issue is that it was done
without the lawful authority or the cons ent of the occupier and owner, because
sometimes it is actually quite hard to te ll the difference. There have been some
delightful stories of magnificent graffiti art th at has been in galleries around the world,
and suddenly the cleaners have come in and cleaned it away. I think we have seen that
people even in our own cities, young pe ople who have been doing tagging and who
have been involved in this so rt of process, are actually quite creative a nd have some
good ideas about art. We have been able to use them and get them out there painting
over things.
The funny thing is that if a graffiti artist ac tually puts a lot of effort into designing a
painting to go over an area that  has been tagged, the chances  are it will not be tagged
again, because if they have got the mana th at they are actually  creating such a good
work, nobody wants to destroy it. In actual fact , in our city, in Christchurch, we have
got several places where they could never control the graffiti, so the neighbourhood got
out and painted them beautifully. One of them  is in the Shirley area, where the rugby—
no, not rugby, but the other one. What is it called?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: League.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: League. That is right, the lea gue club. They had this great big
huge wall that was always being tagged, so in  the end they got out there. They got out
the paint, the whole club painted it, and it has never looked better ever since.
There was one other tweak that we looked at in this bill. We were concerned that the
council be transparent about the authority it  had to access private property to remove
graffiti, and we also wanted to make sure that those contractors were easily identified by
the public. So we actually made some changes to the bill to make that happen.
The final concern was about the council and its liability, or its duty of care towards
those landlords when it is removing graffiti. We did not want to exempt it from taking
reasonable care. We did not think it was ri ght, because contractors across the country
have to take reasonable care otherwise they are liable, and we thought that even though
this is being done for the public good, they still need to do the job properly. Actually, I
think in this case it was probably unnecessary  to put it into the bill, because the
contractor that the council ha s at present is very skilled and does an excellent job. He
matches the paint; he looks af ter the properties. But you ne ver know what is going to
happen in the long term, and I think it was really important to cover that.
In conclusion, this bill was well drafted, a nd the select committee,  with the help of
advisers, managed to get it into shape quickly and efficiently. It was an interesting bill
to work on, and I think we gave a good outcome to the Hutt City Council. As we have
heard, the Hutt City Council does have a really advanced graffiti eradication
programme. That has had a positive effect on its community, and we hope that this bill
will help support that work. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: It has been a pleasure to work on
this local bill, the Hu tt City Council (Graffiti Remova l) Bill, brought to  this House by
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5393
my friend and colleague Trevor Mallard, who wo rked incredibly hard on this bill along
with the Mayor of Lower Hu tt City, Ray Wallace. In fact, Mayor Wallace campaigned
for this bill before he was elected as mayor . He, at that time, declared war on graffiti
and used it very much as part of his mayoral campaign, and he was determined to
deliver on the promises that he made. I think it  is true to say that this campaign struck a
chord with many of the ratepayers out in the Hutt Valley.
You see, we are not talking about graffiti art. There is a difference between graffiti
and graffiti art, and I have to say I learnt a little bit about this from my friend and former
colleague Stevie Chadwick. You see, Stevie  Chadwick’s nephew is Otis Frizzell, and
Otis Frizzell is now a famous graffiti artist. In  fact, I read some of the stuff that he has
written about it and he says that graffiti art is basically the visual representation of hip
hop. Well, I do not claim to understand either graffiti art or hip hop, but I do know it is a
genre that is admired and sought after in the art world. So we are not talking about some
of the amazing murals that have been painted around Wellington by young people in a
graffiti art style. No, we ar e talking in this bill about unwanted, ugly scrawl painted by
unthinking, uncaring, selfish louts who have no hesitation in defacing people’s property
for no reason.
I have to say that I do not know wh ether it has occurred on your property, Mr
Speaker, but it drives people mad. They beco me incredibly angry when they get up in
the morning and they go out and find that their beautifully painted garage door has now
got something that is incomprehensible scrawled all over it.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Sometimes it’s comprehensible.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Well, yes, sometimes it is comprehensible and cannot be
repeated in this House. This happened, just  as you heard from the previous speaker,
Nicky Wagner, on my garage not very long  ago. The annoying thi ng is that you have
got to go out and buy a pot of  paint if you have not had your  garage painted for a while.
You have got to take time to clean it up. It is an intrusion and it is an invasion of your
personal space. It is unsightly, and I have to say I can find no  redeeming features of this
sort of graffiti. People actually hate it.
People particularly hate graffiti that remain s in the same place and is not removed in
a timely fashion. If you are driving around to  the airport and you get opposite Kilbirnie
Park and see a building on the corner there, ha ve a look at the graffiti. It will be cleaned
off, then graffiti will go up. If  it is not removed within a few days, it has numerous tags
all over it. It is unsightly and makes the pe ople in that area of my  electorate feel very
unsafe. It does attract other graffiti, which is why councils, in particular, want to clean it
up as fast as possible. They do not want it remaining. Of course, the graffiti writer wants
as many people as possible to see it. The opposite is true fo r those who have had their
property covered in graffiti and for councils.
So this bill is about empowering Hutt City  Council to remove gr affiti that is on
private property where the owner cannot be foun d or identified in order to give consent,
or, for that matter, to decline consent. It is  not about forcing this on owners; actually, if
an owner declines, it will not be remove d. But it does give the council the opportunity
using an established process to remove graffiti on private property. It is easy for a
council to go along and remove graffiti fr om public property, and they do that
incredibly well. We heard from people from Hutt City that they feel that they have faced
a lot of tagging in their area. They believe that they are probably one of the most tagged
places in New Zealand and so they want to see it removed as fast as possible. They want
it removed off public property, but they also want it removed off private property. So
what Trevor Mallard’s bill does is set out a process for doing this.
As you heard from the chair of our Local  Government and Environment Committee,
we had a very small number of submissions. In fact, there were only seven submissions
5394 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
on this bill, but they were very useful submissions, indeed. From them came some
useful suggestions, including cl arifying the purpose statement to  make it clear that it is
about the removal of graffiti that is on priv ate property and it must be visible from a
public place. So if there is graffiti that is at the back of a property, inside a porch, or
whatever, and cannot be seen, that is not wh at they are talking about. They are talking
about graffiti that is visible in a public place.
The second amendment was about requiri ng the council to state on its graffiti
removal notice the source of the power it was relying upon. Of course, the source of the
power they are relying on is this bill when  it is passed. It also requires council workers
when cleaning up graffiti to be easily identified as to who they are and what they are
doing, because people do get ve ry worried if th ey see people wandering on to their
property with a paintbrush and a can of pain t. They probably think that they are facing
another round of graffiti, so council work ers need to ensure that they are easily
identified when they are cleaning up graffiti.
The minor amendments that the committee made have, I think, improved this bill and
we end up with a bill that I now know that quite a number of councils around New
Zealand are very interested in emulating. They would like to have this  tool in their tool
box for the cleaning up of graffiti on priv ate property. I notice that the Mayor of
Wellington only a week or so ago said how mu ch she would like to have a similar bill.
It was interesting that her officials then we nt on to say: “Oh, yes, but we’d have to
estimate the cost.” Well, that is true, we must  always know the cost of things, but if we
do not clean up graffiti in a timely manner, ther e is a cost to that community. There is a
cost to the feeling of security within that community, and there is a cost to the look of
that community, and to the individual and th eir personal property in the devaluing of
that property. So, yes, we need to be mindful of cost, but we also need to ensure that we
can do whatever is possible to make the e nvironment that people live in pleasant and
safe. We all know that graffiti can ensure people feel unsafe within their communities.
I want to commend Trevor Mallard and the Hu tt City Council, in particular Ray
Wallace, for bringing this bill to the House. Is  it not lovely that we are discussing this
bill in an adult manner on Women’s Suffrage Day? Would it not be nice if many more
of our debates could be so ci vilised rather than some of the ranting and raving that we
heard from people like Simon Bridges and Judith  Collins today? It is nice to be able to
say that here is an agreed piece of legislati on that we want to see go through the House.
I certainly, along with the Labour Party, support this bill.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Good on Ray Wallace, the Mayor of Hutt
City, for campaigning on this issue of graffiti in his community. Good on him for taking
a stand, for putting his head above the para pet and actually standing for something, and
then, when he became the Mayor of Hutt Cit y, following through on it, with the help of
the local member. So good on him, because  at the start of a good community is good
leadership. Clearly, the Hutt City Council ha s got good leadership at local government
level.
A number of members in the House this af ternoon have talked about the impact of
graffiti on an individual. Of course, it is te rrible to have your fence or your garage
graffitied, particularly if it is one of those roller doors that  have corrugated iron. What a
pain to have to organise to get it fixe d because somebody without a care in the world
has come along and decorated it on your behalf. And actually that—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: It’s the cedar ones that are a problem.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Sorry?

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: It’s the cedar ones that are a problem, because you can’t clean them.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: The cedar ones, yes, yes. The me mber from over the other side is
absolutely right: the cedar ones are much, mu ch worse. I do not know whether the local
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5395
authority—and the member might be able to  help me out—would fix that. Is the Hutt
City Council going to come along and strip down a cedar gara ge door, oil it, varnish it,
and return it?

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: That’s a good point.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: The member raises an interesti ng point, and I look forward to his
contribution. It sounds like an expensive solution to me.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No, they won’t damage it.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, I think we will just stick to the roller door example, because
that, I suspect, is more typical of the type of surface that is being graffitied.
It is irritating to the extreme to an individual to have their private property defaced in
this way. But I think also we need to be mindful of the impact on the wider community.
It is absolutely true to say that a public pl ace that has been graffitied and left sends the
message that it is not a safe place for the comm unity, that it is not a place that is cared
for by the community. Indeed, it sends th e message that the community does not
particularly care about its pub lic places. So I come back and again congratulate Mayor
Wallace and his council on, obviously, supporting the passage of this Hutt City Council
(Graffiti Removal) Bill to deal to these issues.
I suspect I have said this to the House but I am going to say it again. I recall when the
Local Government and Environment Comm ittee visited Counties Manukau. We had a
look at a little corner village, which comprised a number of shops and a number of flats.
It was a meeting-place for the community. with  residential areas all around it. That area
was terrible. Apart from the graffiti there was long grass, there was rubbish, and it was
clearly untidy and unkempt. The graffiti was te rrible. A lot of it was indecipherable and
some of it was obscene. Clearly, it was not a good signal to any of the local community.
As part of the select comm ittee visit, we heard about how the local police and the
community, including the council, were getting together and dealing to that graffiti and
dealing to that little corner community. Now it not only is perceived to be a safer place
but is, in fact, a safer place for people of all ages to go and do their shopping, or go and
meet, or do whatever they do—go to the local park. So as we ll as the individual impact
of graffiti there is that wider message to the community.
The Local Government and Environment Committee worked in a very collegial way
on this bill. It made a couple of minor amen dments, which have been rehearsed already
in the House today. With those words I wa nt to congratulate once again Ray Wallace.
Good local leadership is really a signifi cant thing for a community. In doing that, I
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise and speak on the
third reading of the Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill. I was not the Green Party
member who was lucky enough to follow this bill through the select committee process.
That was my colleague Holly Walker, who previously congratulated the Hutt City
Council on its efforts to swiftly deal with vandalism but also—and this is important—to
channel the creativity of young people into street art and positive graffiti art projects.
I think that a major concern of the Green Part y, when we first looked at this bill, was
the potential for the bill to dissuade more positive, artistic graffiti, of which there is
plenty. It can certainly enhance the charact er of towns and citie s to have artistic
graffiti—street art—like in the many laneways of Melbourne and the work of Banksy in
London and around the world. So it is really, really critical that we do not lump all
forms of graffiti into the same basket and say that it is necessarily a bad thing. I think it
was a significant contribution that my co lleague Holly Walker made on the Local
Government and Environment Committee to ensure that there was a satisfactory
definition of “graffiti” in this bill. It makes clear that art with the consent of the property
owner is not graffiti for the purposes of this bill. The select committee also removed the
5396 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
clause that would have exempted the council and its contractors from  civil liability, if
they caused damage while removing the graffiti. There were a number of positive
amendments made to the bill during the select committee process and as it went through
the House. Those changes allowed us to fully support this bill today.
As previous speakers have noted, tagging can be quite a negative element within
society, and it can lead to something that is known as the broke n windows effect. We
have noted that in urban areas where broken windows are not repaired in sufficient time,
or there are ugly scrawls on pieces of propert y—and clearly they are not street art—it
contributes to a negative feeling in the area. It tends to undermine a sense of community
cohesion, and can in fact lead to spiralling social problems, whet her they be further
vandalism or other sorts of crime and violence.
Basically, we want our towns and cities to be places where everybody feels welcome.
Obviously, tagging is not a form of street art,  it is not something that makes people feel
welcome. If it cannot be cleaned up quickly, then it can lead to a sense th at this place is
not looked after and it is not a place where peopl e are welcome. That can lead to further
antisocial behaviour.
As I understand it, tagging is a particular pr oblem in the Hutt, and the area has some
of the highest rates within the country. Tagging tends to proliferate swiftly if it is not
removed. But the Hutt City Council has been very proactive in removing tagging. It has
a dedicated team and a programme, which we have heard has been working very well.
We congratulate the council on this.
Now that the council will have the legal right that this bill creates, it will be able to
take its capacity and willingness to remove unwelcome graffiti or tagging to private
property as well. This will be a very pos itive development for the community. The
intent is not that the council would enter private property and remove graffiti if the
owner wants the graffiti, as I previously  mentioned. That was a very positive
amendment that was made to the bill. Also, owners can respond within 10 working
days, which may not seem particularly impor tant, but it is an amendment from just 10
days. It allows greater time for owners to  take this option, to  say: “Thanks, but no
thanks.” I think it is importa nt that the council respect the property owner’s right to
have that response.
I have heard some of the speakers here today describe taggers as being quite
selfish—people who go out and vandalise priv ate property. That may be one way to
characterise them, but I think that it is wo rth thinking a little b it about why it is that
some young people, or some pe ople generally, do not feel like they are part of the
community, and whether there are better ways to  deal with the sour ces of the problem,
rather than the symptom. Ultimately, taggi ng is just a symptom of a group of people
who do not feel like they are part of society, do not feel that they  have any particular
reason to respect the rights of  others. Within their own p eer group and social group it is
considered a sign of daring or bravery to go ou t and flout the law and to put their tag on
a building or a piece of private property.
I think that there is incredible scope for community building projects—which the
Green Party would support—that would enable young people, people who feel
disenfranchised and feel like they are not part  of society, to have activities that do not
result in this destructive vandalism of private propert y, and also cause the ongoing
ensuing social impacts that I mentioned before. I think there is great potential there, and
I think it would be sad if we wrote off pe ople who are currently tagging as people who
could not become constructive members of  society and channel their passion, their
bravery, and their willingness to flout the law into something more successful.
[Interruption] I was not suggesting that the Hon Tre vor Mallard said that, but I did hear
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5397
other people say that today in the House.  Other members characterised the people who
are currently tagging as louts. I thought that was just a bit unfortunate.
I think it is really important that we cons ider that the society we have now does not
give equal opportunity to everyone to participate, and I think it is worth us reflecting on
the fact that if we understand better the causes of why people behave in antisocial ways,
we might be able to deal with that behavi our in a more constructive way that does not
result in continually having to paint over tags. It is not really a very sustainable response
if we constantly have to go back and pain t over tags, which are going to continue
happening as long as people feel like that is the only way they can go out and assert
their mana.
When Parliament last considered graffiti removal legislation—and that was the
Manukau City Council (Control of Graffiti) Bill—the Green Party opposed it because it
contained all manner of Draconian provision s, including restrict ing young people from
purchasing spray cans. We were  in favour of provisions like  the ones in this bill that
allow removal from private property, provi ded that the civil liability clause was
changed. So although we are very happy to support this bill, I do not think it can be
assumed that we would support similar legislation for other councils around the country.
I think it is really important  that we take them on a case  by case basis and make sure
that the provisions that are made for councils to deal with unwelcome tagging on private
property are proportionate to the particular problems they are facing in each community.
In summary, I am very happy to commend this bill to the House. I congratulate the
member on bringing it before us. We congratulate the Hutt City Council on its proactive
approach to ensure that negative tagging is  not causing continuing spirals of antisocial
behaviour in the Hutt, and also on having proactive programmes in  place to try to
channel the art and the creativity of young peopl e in the streets. The Hutt may be a long
way from the laneways of Melbourne, but ther e is always the potential to channel that
creative energy into some pretty outstanding street art, even in the Hutt. Thank you.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Malo e lelei, Mr Speaker. Thank you very much.
On a day when we celebrate women getting the vote here in New Zealand, and when we
have had many tributes to women who have contributed to New Z ealand, I would like
to begin by celebrating, or paying tr ibute to, two men, the first one being—
[Interruption] Not you, Trevor. You will come second; you are not first. The first one is
the Hutt City Mayor, Ray Wallace, who o bviously has been in touch with his
community and spoken to his ratepayers a nd business owners and has recognised the
enormous concern, anger, and frustration that his constituents have with the problem of
graffiti. As another member pointed out ear lier in this debate, he has gone out and
campaigned on that issue during the local body elections. He has won the mayoralty and
turned his campaign promise and words into action, partnered with the second
individual I would like to pay tribute to, the Hon Trevor  Mallard, the MP for Hutt
South, who has brought this bill, the Hutt Ci ty Council (Graffiti Remo val) Bill, to the
House. That is enough. I will continue now.
I am absolutely amazed about where some of these taggers can  do their tagging. If
anyone has driven south on State Highway 1 in Wellington and seen the rail bridge
across Ngauranga Gorge, some of these pe ople—the louts, or “the sneaky little
bastards” as Trevor Mallard has termed them—some of these youngsters, have actually
gone on to that bridge and tagged it. We really have to wonder about the common sense
of going up on to some of those public places  and tagging. If it were a council staff
person who had to go and clean that up, or maybe KiwiRail, you would have to do a
pretty serious health and safety assessment before you went up there. Some of our
youngsters who are out there doing some of th is stuff are putting themselves at serious
risk of harm when they are doing this tagging on public and private property.
5398 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
This is a bill that, as I said in my second reading speech, should after time, if it
works, be extended to other jurisdictions. I kn ow that certainly in my electorate at the
moment the Mayor of Porirua, Nick Legge tt, is hoping that th is does work on the
ground and that we can crack down on the prevalence of graffiti. In my case, the Porirua
City Council is doing quite a good, proactive j ob of making sure that when graffiti does
go up, whether it be on public land  or whether it be on priv ate land, it is doing a pretty
good job of making sure that it liaises with the property owners or the homeowners to
make sure that it comes down pretty quick smart.
As Trevor Mallard said, there is a sense that there is a serious lack of cohesion within
a community, and a perception of things not being as safe as they should be, when there
is a lot of graffiti in a public area, and cer tainly around our shops. There is certainly one
property in the Porirua area where it has been  an issue. The owner of the building has
not been proactive in making sure that the considerable graffiti that has been on that
building has been taken down quick smart. The community has sent a message pretty
loud and clear that it is not happy with the visuals—or the optics, I should say—of that
extensive graffiti in their neighbourhood because it is br inging down their sense of
community. They do not feel good about that  graffiti being there. And, as has been
mentioned by a number of speakers, there is th e issue of house prices that they certainly
want to take into account. If one were to be selling a house and across the road there
was a building with extensive tagging that had not come down in some time, then you
would be pretty frustrated about the visual pollution that was across the road.
So what this bill does is allow the council to apply to a private property owner where
there is graffiti that is visible from a public place and that property owner has 10 days to
get back to it to ensure that it has the abi lity to go on to that private property, which it
does not have at the moment, and get rid of that  graffiti. I think that is a very pragmatic
approach, and that is why I think there w ill be other councils around the country that
will be watching these measures very clos ely and congratulating the Hutt City Council
and Trevor Mallard on taking this action. They will see this and hope that it works in
Hutt City. I am sure that Trevor Mallar d, Ray Wallace—and Chris Hipkins, who is in
the Hutt as well—

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: And me.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Of course—and Parekura Horomia.  They hope that this measure
works—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: And Rino Tirikatene.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: —and Rino Tirikatene, and I think most MPs—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Charles Chauvel.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: —and Charles Chauvel. I thin k most councils around the country
will be looking at this experi ence and hoping that it works for them and that it can be
extended out to their situation, as well.
I think I speak on behalf of most members of  Parliament when I say that we are all
probably victims of graffiti, whether it be on our electorate offices or every 3 years
when we put up our hoardings and the carniva l of the campaign begins. I think it would
be very rare that there was any member of this House or any candidate at any election
who has not been a victim of graffiti. I had one case where I put a hoarding on my
house and 45 minutes later, less than an hour later, one of these—and I will not refer to
them how Trevor Mallard referred to them—youngsters, I am assuming, was there—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Sneaky little bastards.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: —I will not use that term—and had obviously seen that I had put
up this hoarding at the front of my house, and within the hour had shown his artistic
abilities on one of my hoardings. I managed to rub it out, using nail polish remover, but
the very next day he was back again—
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5399

items.speaker: Hon Chris Tremain
items.text: Out of your back pocket.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Do not ask me where I got the na il polish remover from. The very
next day the very same person had been back obviously, because I recognised the tag
that was on the hoarding. On behalf of all members of Parliament and candidates for
office, we all share in the pain of those pe ople who have been victims of graffiti. No
doubt in a couple of years’ time, when we go back to that phase of  democracy, we will
be back out there trying to repair some of the damage that has been done to our
hoardings.
I would like to take this opportunity to pay tr ibute to some of the local heroes in the
Porirua area who have been working for ma ny, many years to make sure that they
eradicate graffiti from around the city. Most of them are from a programme run by the
Porirua City Council, and I would just like  to mention Charlie Devenish and Miranda
Pittaway, who was formerly from Housing Ne w Zealand Corporation. They did great
work in making sure that they identified public places and put up tag-resistant murals in
those areas. I am thinking of the mural in Ha mpshire Street, which I had the pleasure of
helping to paint, and also on Mungavin Avenue, close to Holy Family School. It is those
kinds of projects, as Julie Anne Genter sa id, that we should be focusing on. We should
be beautifying those areas where taggers target, making sure we see the positive in this,
and turning them into areas that we celebra te and make sure that they are visually
stimulating. Then, I think, it sends the message  out to those who might want to tag it
that they should stay right away from it or suffer the consequences.
I pay tribute to the former graffiti mana gement coordinator from the Porirua City
Council, Trevor Mason, who worked very ha rd and has now retire d from that role. He
did very, very good work in terms of eradicatin g graffiti. I also pay tribute to the group
known as WAG, the Waitangirua Action Group, which is a bunch of very hard-working
mothers who go out and paint out a lot of the graffiti very quickly, as soon as it is put up
in the Porirua East area. I also need to mention Liana Leiataua and Lepeti Tea, who
have worked as coordinators as well, to make sure graffiti is stamped out in the Porirua
area, and John Poppleton, who used to be with Keep Po rirua Beautiful, and who has
also worked hard to keep Porirua looking as beautiful as can be.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to fo llow Kris Faafoi, except I
felt it was an unfortunate start to his speech  when I saw Mr Mallard sitting forward in
anticipation and expectation when Kris said  that he was going to congratulate a number
of people, and he turned and said “But not you, Trevor.”

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Not yet.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Not yet. But I have never seen such a look of
disappointment and a feeling of rejection. So  I would like to begi n, and have it on
record, that I congratulate th e Hon Trevor Mallard on bringi ng this bill, the Hutt City
Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill, and shepherd ing it through the House, because it is a
wonderful achievement and he should be pleased with the success that he has had.
I would like to perhaps introduce a slightly lighter look to graffiti, because everyone
so far has been dealing with the heavy and ve ry serious aspects of it. I do not wish to
take that away, but I do remember—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Kilroy was here.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: My opening phrase—“Kilroy was here”—because I
knew—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: We remember.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I knew there would be someone who would remember.
“Stop the war. Yanks go home.”—in my childhood that was about it, although on the
West Coast there are some old graffiti signs saying “Cantabrians, don’t get your
whitebait over here.”, and that sort of thi ng. But for the most part graffiti was always
5400 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
very occasional. It was not a feature when I was being brought up. But then I remember,
when we moved to Christchurch, there was a garage door in Fendalton that had a new
sign on it every week—quite nicely painted and quite nicely done, but it was a pithy sort
of statement like “If the world isn’t flat, w hy do we keep trying to blow it up?”. It was
quite the talk of the community. We wondered what the phrase was going to be the next
week. And then there was a group of people in the flat who clearly had feminist views.
It was mostly anti-men, but, again, it was amusing, it was witty. Then there was a long
period of absence when either they had a te nant who did not want to write anything, or
they did not have a tenant at all. The fo llowing week when you went past it was empty,
and by the end of the week someone else ha d written on it “Say something”, because
people were used to seeing that as they drove past.
But for the most part tagging is a negative experience, and I have heard of incidences
today of how communities have been really  working hard—hit it hard, as soon as it
occurs—to get rid of it as s oon as it occurs. Those people to o are to be congratulated. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I will take a third call on behalf of New
Zealand First on the Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill.  Can I just say that in
looking at the background to Hutt City, it is  very interesting to study this wonderful—
relatively small by international standards, but a lovely size by New Zealand
standards—city. It is interesting that on Women’s Suffrage Day, where the women have
had the vote for 119 years, a bill affecting a small city in New Zealand would be getting
its third and final reading th rough the House and showing wh at local democracy is all
about in this country. At times I am su re many New Zealanders do ask what is
happening with local democracy in this country, when you look—

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Certainly after what’s happened in Christchurch.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: —exactly—at what has ha ppened in Canterbury, when
you look at the steamroller th at went through Auckland, wh en you look at the third,
fourth, and fifth-largest citi es in New Zealand being put out of existence in Auckland,
with virtually no public  consultation and, certainly, no referendum, and where you still
have a city like Hutt City, which is able to  still function fully with full democracy, full
local democracy, and getting on with the job, as we heard before, but getting on with the
job, in this case, of bringing a good thing to its people and to its community.
When I look at Hutt City an d I see that it prides itse lf on the fact that it has
something like 25 parks, 50 playgrounds, six swimming pools, ei ght public libraries,
two museums, and the best beaches in the Wellington region, then, obviously, it is great
to see that it is bringing forward a bill to reduce graffiti. It has so many public places,
and it has so many areas where it does not wa nt to be seeing, from recreational and
public places, what is basically very antisocial graffiti on the walls of private properties
adjoining public spaces. It also mentions that Hutt City has 10 secondary schools, 50
primary schools, and 40 early childhood centr es. They have a lot of young people in
Hutt City. They have a lot of  young people who are very gr eatly influenced by their
surroundings and their urban environment. If they grow up in an urban environment that
is cluttered with graffiti and nasty, antisoc ial scrawlings on many of the faces of the
walls and buildings around Hutt City, what sort of environment is that for them to grow
up in? So it is a great thing that the Hutt City Council, with the Hon Trevor Mallard
championing it, has brought this bill to this  Chamber and to this House to have it put
through. A proud city that evolved from the Hutt County Council from 1877, and in
1941 became Hutt City Council—1941; that is quite a long time ago—it now has
something like 102,000 residents and is in the to p 10 largest cities of this country. So it
is very good.
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5401
I was certainly on the Local Government and Environment Committee and was very
supportive of this initiative th at it had to try to remove un wanted graffiti from private
properties where it could not have that done, where, perhaps, landlords were absentee
landlords overseas, or uncar ing landlords, or people who simply took no interest in
maintaining the properties—we went through stringent requirement s with the select
committee to ensure that they would still be given adequate notice, several weeks’
notice, to remove the graffiti and go through all the usual legalities of serving correct
notice on the property owners—so that, at th e end of the day, if the council wants to
step in and remove some of that nasty gr affiti from some of the structures around its
city, which it has great pride in, it could do so.
So, also, I would like to recognise Mayor Ray Wallace and his city councillors, and
the executive and staff of Hutt City Council,  who have worked this through. I am sure
there will be many other city councils and ot her local authorities in New Zealand that
will wish to do the same. Indeed, I can see that Wellington City Council itself would
like to do the same. Hutt City is the second- largest city in the Wellington region. I have
no doubt that others like Wellington City, Porirua, and others, will want to follow suit in
due course, particularly when they see the significant difference that this can make in
the region.
I have mentioned in the House before that when I was Mayor of North Shore, we had
a problem for many years, and we got on top of  it. It was costing us in the order of
$600,000-odd a year for graffiti and vandalism, but  we put in place a team to get on top
of the problem—former policemen, incidental ly, who came to work for the council;
retired policemen—who started to profile the taggers, started to work out who they
were, and started to keep a very comprehens ive database of the regular taggers. When
the taggers were appr ehended by the Waitemat ā District Police a nd we could put two
and two together and identify who the culprits  were in each instance, it had significant
effects on having them desist and cease thei r activities, but also on getting some
restitution from those offenders. Where restitutio n was not possible, they certainly were
put through the mill and had to undertake community work. In many cases the
community work included removing not only many of their own tags but also other
people’s tags to give them a good lesson in  having some respect for other people’s
property.
In respect of this, however, we in New Z ealand First are somewhat concerned that
perhaps this is, in a sense, the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, in that this is fixing
the graffiti at the end of the day once it is there, rather than, perhaps, preventing it
before it even gets there.  And that comes back to th e education of  our young people—
good schooling, good upbringing, and, you know, good tuition fr om their teachers and
from the parental guidance that they get, wh ich is most important in this country. But
also it comes back to resources within our police and our authorities to be able to ensure
that people can get on top of this and the police can actually provide a presence in many
of these communities so that this does not o ccur. Because, at the end of the day, if there
is not much of a police presence in our communities, you can end up with antisocial
behaviour, and often the antiso cial behaviour goes hand in  hand with the likes of
graffiti, tagging, and vandalism, and often th at in turn leads to much more serious
crime. At the end of the day, if we can knock it on the head before it even gets to that
stage, with greater police resources, so much the better.
In that regard I was very pleased that a number of years ago New Zealand First was
the party that helped push through this H ouse—this is a number of years ago under a
Labour Government—a measure to get another thousand police on the beat around New
Zealand. A thousand more police on the beat, under the Labour Government, supported
by the initiative from New Zealand First to  do that, negotiated by Rt Hon Winston
5402 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
Peters, to get a thousand more police out th ere in our communities. These are the sorts
of resources that are needed around our country to ensure that this happens.
On another note we also need to have sa feguards, and one of the safeguards with
graffiti and vandalism is ensuring that the source  of the materials used is also restricted.
In that respect restricting access to aerosol cans and keeping them in DIY stores, in
dairies, and in other places in locked cabinets so that nobody  can just walk in and grab
one off the shelf, or steal it, or try to get away with it as a young minor—these are the
sorts of things that we do have to do to ensure that we restrict the access. Obviously,
they have to use something to deface a fen ce, a wall, a house, a bu ilding, or whatever,
and often it is aerosol paints that are used. So restricting access to those is very, very
important.
In closing, can I just again commend all thos e who are involved with this. This is a
good initiative. This is local government doing what local g overnment is good at. It is
bringing the concerns of its people, of its citizens, and of its communities to this
Parliament, and it is getting things done. Th is is allowing local government to speak on
behalf of its people. This is ensuring that on the 119 th anniversary of women’s suffrage
and giving women the vote, a local voice is he ard, in the Hutt City Council and in this
Parliament from the Hutt City Council. We certa inly want to ensure that this sort of
local democracy, local government, contin ues through all the communities of New
Zealand and is not steamrolled out of existe nce by a National Government that really
has very, very little interest in supporting the second tier of government in this country,
a most important tier of government in this country, which, basically, is the glue for our
communities to operate. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Sometimes in this House there are some
things that are really hard to say. I am going to attempt one right now: Good on Trevor
Mallard for bringing this bill, the Hutt City  Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill, into the
House. I hope I do not have to  say that too often in my time here. This is a good little
piece of legislation that Trevor Mallard has helped to shepherd through for the Hutt City
Council. Congratulations also to the Hutt City Council on propos ing it, and to the
mayor, Ray Wallace.
I will just be very brief here, because it is  a simple bill and one that seems to have a
lot of support around the House.  Graffiti is a scourge on the local communities. It is
something that locals dislike a lot. When it comes to graffiti on private property, it can
be difficult for councils to clean it up, and fo r those who have their property graffitied
on a regular basis, it can be time-consuming, and it can be costly for them to clean it up.
So enabling the local authority to have th e power to go in, afte r giving the property
owner notice to go and clean it up, is a good thi ng, indeed. My only regret is that this is
not actually a nationwide piece of  legislation, because I think it would be quite good as
a nationwide one.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: We’ve got a lazy Government.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Perhaps if we have some d ecent member’s bill ideas coming
forward from the other side of the House—th ey could consider that for their members’
bills, rather than some of the things that ar e going to actually cost people jobs, and cost
employers their ability to employ people. This bill is a good one. I support it and hope
that it gets through unanimously.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the ne xt call is a split
call. I will ring the bell at 4 minutes.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That was a very insightful call from
Jami-Lee Ross. It is not often that we get National members standing up in the House
and delivering such honest appraisals of their own Government’s performance, as we
just saw from Jami-Lee Ross, who was condemning his own Government for not
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5403
picking up the principle behind this piece of legislation, the Hutt C ity Council (Graffiti
Removal) Bill, and making it a national bill. Th at was effectively what he just did. He
took only 30 seconds to do it, and it was a ve ry accurate appraisal of the Government’s
performance on this issue.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: They need the Opposition on this bill.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That is right. It needs the Opposition to do it. I do take great
pleasure in rising to speak in fa vour of this particular piece of legislation in the name of
my colleague Trevor Mallard. I know that he  has put a huge amount of work into this
piece of legislation, and I only hope that in a bout 25 years’ time, after I have also been
in Parliament for the equivalent length of time as Mr Mallard, I too may have a bill such
as the Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill passed through the House in my name.
But, perhaps on a more serious note, I do want to acknowledge the Hutt City
Council, although I have a problem with that in  one respect. I grew up in Lower Hutt. I
do not know where this place Hutt City is. Actually, if you go to the New Zealand
Geographic Board, it does not know where Hutt  City is, either. There is Lower Hutt,
and there is Upper Hutt, and in the not too distant past some empire-building mayor in
Lower Hutt decided that he was going to rename Lower Hutt as Hutt City. There is
actually no such place as Hutt  City. And I can say that because I was born there and I
grew up there. I do not know where this place Hutt City actually is. It is Lower Hutt, it
has always been Lower Hutt, and it is still Lo wer Hutt. So that is ju st a little bit of my
pet peeve for the day, which I just wanted to get off my chest. Now that I have done
that, I want to turn a little bit more to the substance of the bill.
Graffiti has been a problem in the Hutt Valley, not just in Lower Hutt but in Upper
Hutt as well, and this piece of legislation will allow the Lower Hutt council, or the Hutt
City Council as it prefers to call itself, to remove graffiti from private property in certain
circumstances. I just want to put into context what we are talking about here. We are not
necessarily talking about gara ge doors, because in the case of a garage door on
somebody’s house, it is not that difficult fo r the council to go and knock on their door
and say “Hey, you’ve got graffiti there. Can we remove it?”. That is generally not where
the problem begins. The problem begins in bu ildings that are not currently occupied. I
will give an example of an old, empty factory that might back on to the riverbank, for
example. In that case it can take a long tim e to actually figure out who owns it, to get
hold of the owner if there is no tenant at the moment, and say “Actually, do you mind if
we remove the graffiti?”. Of course, in 99 pe rcent of the cases they say “Well, we don’t
really care. Do whatever you like.”, but at the moment it is taking the council a long
time to track down who those owners are and get their permission. What this bill says is
just go ahead and do it. I think that is qui te a reasonable thing for the council to be
doing.
There are buildings in the Hutt Valley where it could take some time to track down
the owners. I know of a building in Upper Hutt that will not be  covered by this
legislation, where the owner is based offshore.  The building is no l onger occupied, it is
vandalised on a regular basis, and the owner actually just does not care. The owner does
not live in New Zealand, does not have to driv e past this particular  property every day,
and just does not care. If that property was in Lower Hutt, under this piece of legislation
the council would be able to do something about that.
