I think it is a welcome initiative. Graffiti is something that simply drives people mad.
It is pointless. It is destructive. It is th e destruction of people’ s private properties. I
really feel for some of the residents in my neighbourhood, actually, in Trentham, who I
see out there painting their fen ces or waterblasting their fences on a fairly regular basis.
It must be infuriating for them to have to get out there and repaint their fences after
these little toe-rags basically get out there and—
5404 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Toe-rags?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —that is right—vandalise their fences. But, actually, where I
think there is another problem area, which I do not think this bill necessarily addresses
and which we are seeing incr easingly throughout the Hutt Valley, is etching. Etching of
glass windows costs a heck of a lot more for local businesses than painting. Painting can
be removed with a bit of turps. Etching is very, very expensive, and that is something
that I think we need to find some solutions to  as well. I know that it is costing our local
businesses—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry to interrupt the honourable
member.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I am pleased to take a brief call to reaffirm the
Greens support for this bill, the Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill. At the risk of
further offending Mr Hipkins’ sensibilities, I will refer to the Hutt City Council, given
that it is the entity in w hose name this bill is. It do es deserve congratulations,
particularly to the mayor, who I understand has provided some real leadership on this to
get the solution to this point where the bill is being passed into law.
I do not pretend to know either Upper Hutt or  Lower Hutt well. Certainly, I have no
particular close experience of them. But having up until quite recently lived much of my
life in Auckland City, I am no stranger to graffiti or to the significant cost that is
imposed visually, socially, a nd, not least of all, economical ly. I think there would be a
very strong case to encourage other councils to pick up a si milar piece of  legislation,
and for this House to create some sort of general law that would enable other councils to
resolve the issue of entering on to private la nd to remove this unsightly blot on the
landscape, which graffiti is and always will be.
As I said, I do not know the Hutt particularly well, but I am interested to note that in
the report from the Local Government and Environment Committee comparison was
made with the Auckland rail corridor. I do know a thing or two about the scale of the
problem in that context. I know that KiwiRail, supported by some very able and willing
volunteer groups, has been working incredibly hard to try to clean up the Auckland rail
corridor. So if Hutt City is experiencing the problem on the same scale as that, then it
most certainly does have a problem. Indee d, KiwiRail in Auckland ran up against the
same issue of private buildings  bordering its rail corri dor. It needed to seek permission
to go and actually remove the graffiti there, for the simple reason that it had no absolute
right to deal with that. A bill of this nature, I suspect, would have facilitated that process
for it considerably, and for that reason the bill is to be supported.
The point has been made that the Greens did oppose a previous attempt to manage
graffiti, which was the Manukau solution as it was possessed at the time. We saw that
that was not the path to go down, to eff ectively criminalise young people for simply
carrying marker pens. It was a highly complicated and somewhat punitive approach.
This is a much cleaner, simpler approach. It simply puts the solution in the hands of the
local authority in the community, not without considerable cost, and I acknowledge that,
but over time hopefully we will uncover and apply some longer-term solutions.
Like Mr Auchinvole, I am actually old enough to recall when graffiti really was not
particularly a problem in our ci ties, towns, and elsewhere. It is unfortunate to see that it
has become so ubiquitous, so costly, and so  negative in our communities. In fact, I
recall in the late 1970s, just as a hobby, I did some photogra phic courses and did a little
bit of a photographic essay of some of the graffiti that was around Auckland. Almost
without exception it was social and political  commentary. Some of it was very clever,
some of it was very witty, and some of it was very apt to the political context of the day.
That is not to excuse it or suggest that it is acceptable, but I literally had to go looking
for examples of graffiti, and that was not that long ago. Nowadays, of course, one is
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5405
hard-pressed in many areas or in many commu nities to find a wall that has not been
defaced at some point. We have certainly got to a serious situation with this graffiti.
I think the definition of graffiti in the bill  is good. I think it is  a very useful and
positive addition to the bill—to the legislation—that we are defining very clearly what it
is we are talking about, to avoid the unfort unate incidents where murals—“graffiti art”,
as it is referred to, will be protected. Again, I am not particularly a fan of graffiti art, but
I acknowledge that there are many who do admire  it and appreciate it, and it has proven
to be a very effective mechanism for preventi ng the tagging, the defacing, that we are
seeing far too much of.
As I have said, we need to continue to investigate the root cau ses: youth alienation
and the fact that particular ly youth who perform the taggi ng clearly have no empathy,
no sense of the impact and the negative cost s they are imposing, the social costs, and
making people feel vulnerable if their homes or properties are damaged by graffiti. That
is a much more difficult task. It will take a great deal of work by local government,
community, and other authorities. I commend this bill and the Hutt City Council for this
very useful measure. Kia ora.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: This is a very brief call—the last one from
the National Party benches—that certainly  commends the work of the Hon Trevor
Mallard for a very sensible bill, the Hutt C ity Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill, and also
the Local Government and Environment Committee and the approach it has taken on it.
Just very briefly, Rudi Giuliani, a former  Mayor of New York, coined the phrase
“broken windows”. That was born out of his ap proach to addressing petty crime at the
bottom to bring the murder rate down. What he  established through that was that if the
city got on top of gra ffiti and those jumping the turnstiles to skip a dollar, it actually
drove the homicide rate down and the serious crime rate down. That was something that
was introduced in New Zealand in many police forces across the country. That approach
is very much reflected in this bill. It will not only take care of the unsightly nature of
graffiti and the impact that it has in terms of a community’s sense of pride, safety, and
so forth, but it will actually, I am sure, have  an impact on bringing down other crime
related to it. I have no problem in commending this bi ll and the sponsoring member to
the House. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: As a member of the Local Government and
Environment Committee that considered th is bill, the Hutt Ci ty Council (Graffiti
Removal) Bill, I am very happy to take a call and congratulate my colleague the Hon
Trevor Mallard on shepherding this piece of legislation through the House. He worked
very hard in the select committee, as the conduit between our committee and the Hutt
City Council, to ensure that the changes that we were considering were deemed to be
both acceptable and effective by the Hutt City Council. I think we have ended up with a
piece of legislation that is not only workable but will be very effective in the Hutt City
Council’s fight to eradicate graffiti in its area.
The issue of graffiti and tagging has been  a major issue in Lower Hutt, going back
many, many, many years. This is not a new i ssue. This is not something the council has
only just decided to try to address—a lthough I do note that Mayor Ray Wallace did
make a plank of his election campaign a war on graffiti. Unfortunately, Lower Hutt is
one of the worst areas in the country for ta gging and for graffiti, and given that it is
actually such a lovely part of the Wellington district, anything that serves to better the
image of that community—throughout the rest of Wellington and the country—is
indeed welcome.
Before I came into Parliament, I was a member of the P ētone Community Board in
Lower Hutt. Graffiti was one of the main issues that people brought to us as a
community board. Along with the protection of  heritage buildings, one of the biggest
5406 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
issues that our community faced was the is sue of tagging and graffiti. People would
come to our community board meetings whe n, for example, there was a public building
or a private residence that was significantly damaged, significantly graffitied, and say
that they could not understand why nothing was being done about it. When they came to
us, we would liaise with council officers.
What we often found were the very proble ms that have led to this piece of
legislation, which are that often the peopl e who owned the buildings were absentees;
they were not there. Often they had not been  paying rates, so it was clear that they had
basically just departed from the district, and really had no more interest in the upkeep of
that building. In the case of private buildings, sometimes they were dealing with
tenants, who were not able to either fi x it themselves—did not have the financial
means—or felt that under the law, under reside ntial tenancy legislation, it should be the
landlord’s responsibility to do that work.
Whereas the council could often get the appr oval of the tenants, getting the approval
of the landlords who actually owned the prope rty was sometimes very, very difficult to
do. We often ended up in the situation of having to say to them that we did not have the
right to just walk on to someone’s property and make alterations; we could not find the
people who own the building, we could not find the people who lease the building, and,
therefore, our hands were really tied. That , obviously, does not go  down particularly
well with the members of the community w ho pay rates and who feel very proud of
their community, and who get very disturbed and upset when they see buildings being
defaced in the way that, unfortunately, they have been throughout Lower Hutt, and, in
fact, throughout the country.
I think the comment that this is perhaps something that could be picked up by other
councils is very pertinent. But as a member  of the Local Government and Environment
Committee, which has an enormous amount of legislation before it, we would probably
rather see one Government bill than 60 di fferent local government bills coming to our
committee on this issue. So maybe it is some thing that the Government could pick up,
to see whether or not there is a need a nd a demand for it thr oughout the rest of the
country. As I said, our committee has done th e work on it. Trevor Mallard has done the
work on it. Certainly, the Hutt City Council and the issues, historically, that it has been
facing with tagging and graffiti provided a very good basis for developing this
legislation. I think it will be very easy to pi ck it up and roll it out throughout the rest of
the country.
There are many reasons why this is an impor tant issue. It might not seem like a big
issue to some people, but serious issues of tagging and graffiti do affect property values
for those people who live in the community around them. If someone sees an area where
there is an enormous amount of tagging, wh ere there may be a row of buildings owned
by someone who is not present in the distri ct and is not contac table, it can send a
message out about that community that is ve ry negative, which may affect the property
values of other people around th em, even if, in fact, that ne gative perception is not true.
And so, in terms of the rights  of other property owners in that area, this is a very
important piece of legislation for them.
But I think one of the biggest reasons why th is is important is that the quick removal
of tagging, in particular, but graffiti in general, provide s a strong disincentive against
doing it again. What we know is that the longe r it is left there, the longer the taggers—
the people who are doing the graffiti—can get th e satisfaction of seeing it, and the more
likely they are to try to do it again or get th e message that if they do it, it is something
that is going to be there long term; that no one is going to do anything about it, and they
can brag about it. The quicker you get rid of it and make it clear that as soon as it goes
19 Sep 2012 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 5407
up it is coming down, then the quicker they will lose interest in going to those buildings
and carrying out this particular destructive activity.
I want to note that the Hutt City Council has been dealing with this for a long time. It
has a graffiti eradication officer. The counc il has been spending up to half a million
dollars a year on graffiti removal in its community. The council, through its graffiti
eradication officer, has been working with the community. So this is not simply just an
approach of “This is the only thing we are going to do, and the minute it goes up, we are
going to take it down.” The council has been  engaging with the community and trying
to address the underlying issues in those communities that lead to this antisocial
behaviour, that lead to this de structive behaviour. That is a very important part of the
equation, because times are very tough.
Unfortunately, when times get really tough, often we  see an increase in these levels
of antisocial behaviour. I would hate to see th is bill not being seen in the context of the
very difficult economic times in which we  find ourselves. Putting it back on the
Government members, a number of whom have made very positive comments about
this piece of legislation, we certainly welcome their support for it, but I just say to them
to not ever forget that the Government has a role in ensuring that we can have the kind
of economy and the kind of community that does not lead to vast increases in antisocial
behaviour because of economic hardship. Ce rtainly, I know that around the country we
have seen increases in antisocial behaviour. Do  not take it out of context. Do not think
that this bill is fixing it. This is actually a much, much bigger problem.
Sometimes I think we can get ourselves in to this little bubble of this piece of
legislation and lose sight of th e big picture, which is that we  need to deal with the core
causes of antisocial behaviour, of this ki nd of destructive behaviour, by young people
who feel so disconnected from their community  that they can just go out and deface it.
That is a worrying trend that you see. It is  easy to just write th em off and call them
names, and do this, and that, and the other thing. But let us no t be that glib about it, is
all that I would say.
I think you have only to look around the worl d at some of the antisocial behaviour
that is coming out of communities and, in part icular, by young people, to see that there
is something there that needs to be addre ssed. You never excuse the behaviour, but it is
important to try to understand it and see if th ere is something far more serious lying at
the base of it.
The select committee made a number of im portant changes to the legislation. One
was actually to include a definition of “graffiti”. I think, again, it is important to put that
in context. The Hutt City Council made it quite  clear to us that there was not a lot of
grey area in terms of the buildings that it was talking about. There were concerns, and I
think we addressed them at the select comm ittee, around the definition of graffiti, about
where you get that line between graffiti and art.
What the council said to us  was that it was not dealin g with any cases where it
thought anyone would seriously think that it  was art; it was deali ng with cases where it
was clearly tagging, where it was clearly meant to offend, it was clearly meant to
damage, and it was pretty cut and dried. But, yes, having a definiti on in the bill would
mean that if it ever did come up with a ca se, from time to time, where there might be
that line, then it had no problem with that  safety net, if you lik e, being put in the
legislation.
I think in terms of what the Hutt City C ouncil are dealing wit h, and for people who
might be listening to this debate and worrying that we are going to be starting to get into
that area where the lines are blurred, we are no t. What they are trying to deal with in the
Hutt City is clearly graffiti. It is clearly m eant to offend. This legislation will give the
council the ability to deal with that.
5408 Hutt City Council (Graffiti Removal) Bill 19 Sep 2012
We also made it very clear that this is gr affiti in public sight. In terms of extending
the powers of the council to go on to private pr operty, it is where the graffiti is visible
from a public point of view. So if it is right around the back of a house, the council
would not have the right to go around ther e. There were some people who thought the
council should have the right to go all th e way around and remove  graffiti if it was
offensive and if it was meant just to deface. But we were very clear. This is where it is
viewed from a public viewpoint. We were very clear that this is not  about graffiti art,
even though the council was telling us that that is absolutely not a problem.
I want to commend the Hutt City Council. It has done an awful lot of work. It has
done an awful lot of work with utility pr oviders, because power poles and power boxes
are a target for taggers. I just want to acknowledge the huge amount of work that the
council has put in to try to address the problem, without having to come to Parliament to
ask for legislation. It has done amazing wo rk. We find ourselves, along with the
council, saying that it just needs this bit of le gislation for us to get it over the line, so
that we really can declare the war on graffiti that Mayor Wallace said that he was going
to do when he was elected.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on the
Minimum Wage Amendment Bill. In starting, I want to acknowledge the difficulties for
those living on low incomes and on the minimu m wage. The goal is indeed to increase
the minimum wage. Indeed, this Government has done so every year  since it came to
office, as well as reducing the lower tax rate s, including the first marginal tax rate to
10.5 percent and to 17.5 percent for those earning over $14,001, and we have
maintained Working for Families.
I think that is really where any agreement or empathy I have with the sponsor of this
bill ends, because, as I have said in this House in the past, Dr Clark has become very
good at telling half a story very well. One of th em is that this will not have an effect on
businesses, on people on more than the mini mum wage, or on unemployment. I want to
take him to a place where he has never been, and that is into the smoko room of a small
business. Let us say it is a plumbing firm in Dunedin North. He is sitting in a smoko
room, and the story goes something like this: “Hey, guess what, Scott?”.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Tell me what.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: “I was on $13.50 an hour. The Government changed
the law, and now I’m on $15 an hour.” Jami-L ee sits beside him in the smoko room and
he says “Hang on. I was on $15 an hour. I was ahead of you by 11 percent. I’m going to
go to my employer and say that I want an 11 pe rcent increase in that wage.” So he gets
19 Sep 2012 Minimum Wage Amendment Bill 5409
to $16.67 an hour. Then another person in the plumbing firm—her name might be
Louise—is sitting there going “Hang on, I was on $16.67 an hour. I want an 11 percent
increase.” So that person goes to $18.52. And so on and so on. It is simply not
acceptable—in fact, it is deceitful—to say that this would not have a knock-on effect on
the thousands and thousands of small businesses in this country.
Let us remember that the other side talk a bout big business. They talk a lot about big
business, do they not? But we know that nearly  60 percent of employees in this country
are employed by businesses of fewer than—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I apologise for interrupting the
member’s speech, but I have a small business, and none of that happens in my small
business.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sit down. That is not a point of
order. Points of order are about process, not  about content. The member has a chance to
make a contribution to this debate later on if he wishes.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I was saying that this is a country of small businesses.
Nearly 60 percent of employees in this country are employed by businesses employing
fewer than 19 staff. If one takes it up to 50 sta ff, it is nearly 90 percent of all of those
people.
Official advice on this bill has it that 5,500 people would lose their jobs. On this day,
which is Women’s Suffrage Day, the same of ficial advice says that 3,350 of those
people would be women. Dr Clark blogs about the fact that this would not have any
effect, and refers to unemployment rates in the 1990s. He says that Labour increased the
minimum wage significantly and that une mployment went down. If you follow that
logic, why do we not make the minimum wage $30, and unemployment would
disappear? It is voodoo economics, and it does not make sense.
The last thing he has been blogging about is  the Prime Minister’s cleaner. The Prime
Minister’s cleaner, according to Dr Clark, is earning some thing like $14-something an
hour. That is above the minimum wage but still not enough to live on, particularly given
the many dependent children in her care—by so me counts, it could be eight. That is a
challenge. I accept that. But this is another example of the member telling half a story
very well. Thanks to Working for Families and accommodation supplements, somebody
in that situation, even on the minimum wa ge, with that many children in their care,
would be getting the grossed-up equivalent of  a $70,000 salary. I accept that that is an
appropriate thing to do. In fact, anybody in that situation—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: She’s a grandmother.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, that does not mean that those children are not in
her care.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: They are not in her care.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: So this is the point: telling half—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: They’re not.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: That is right. Well, let us say that maybe only four
children are in her care, so probably $60,000. The point is tell the whole story, Dr Clark,
because it does this case no good. At least when Holly Walker talked about Working for
Families in this debate she compared that with a subsidy to employers. I simply do not
agree with that. If you call that  a subsidy and then take it  away from those people who
have family members who need to be cared for and give it to people who do not, that
does not make sense, nor does this bill.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: On behalf of New Zealand First I rise to speak
to the Minimum Wage Amendment Bill. Firs t we have to congrat ulate David Clark on
his good fortune to have his bill actually dr awn from the ballot. New Zealand First
supports a minimum wage of $15 an hour. It was a policy that we actually campaigned
5410 Minimum Wage Amendment Bill 19 Sep 2012
on during the election, and it is great to see the support on this side of the House for this
bill and this very important issue.
In New Zealand First we actually want Kiwis to be able to earn a fair day’s pay for a
fair day’s work, and at the moment too many people—young people, in particular—are
struggling to make ends meet. Since GS T went up in 2010 the minimum wage has
increased only slightly, to $13.50 an hour . We have got 300,000 workers earning the
minimum wage, and we see it in lots of bus inesses right around the country. I know of
service stations where the workers are paid only the minimum wage, when they are the
sole person who is actually on site. In Australia the minimum wage is the equivalent of
NZ$20. I know that this Government has stat ed on many occasions that it is committed
to closing the gaps. This is one way that it  could close the gap w ith our neighbours. We
can really make a start on this issue. As it currently stands, we have got an exodus of
young people moving to Australia for jobs and fo r better wages, and they are going en
masse. Many of them know that they can actually get a fa r better deal over the Ditch
than what they get here.
For months we have seen reports of families struggling to live on the minimum
wage, and we have got one report here, Solutions to Child Poverty in New Zealand ,
from the Expert Advisory Group on Solutions  to Child Poverty. We see reports of
children working after school in jobs in orde r to pay for their school uniforms, because
mum and dad cannot earn enough to actually buy it for them. I have got one such report
here from August 2012 from Stuff, which sa ys that a 16-year-old Auckland schoolboy
“already works 25 hours a week to help keep his siblings in school  … The teenager’s
earnings helped pay for school fees, stationery and uniforms for him and his siblings but
couldn’t cover school trips which they alwa ys missed out on.” This is indicative of
people not having a reasonable living income . We know that child ren are going to
school hungry. We have heard it often, right here in this Parliament, and, of course, that
affects their learning. I know, having come from a school classroom.
Change has to begin with the low-income earne rs, with the battlers. It is these people
who are the glue that keeps our society together. And we can see why people are
packing their bags and head ing over the Ditch. The high wages are a magnet that New
Zealand just cannot compete with—yet we s hould. Wages have not even kept up with
the cost of living. Everything we can think of —petrol, rates, rent, electricity, milk, even
prescription charges—has gone up far faster than wages, yet we have a Government that
has taken few steps to alleviate the pressure  on hard-working Kiwis. I must say that I
was delighted to hear Minister Bridges say in question time this afternoon that he was
reconsidering the registration and the warrant of fitness fees. Anything will help these
working people. What we have got here is the fact that we are left to some of the free-
market ideologues in this Parliament and, qu ite frankly, with them  there would be no
minimum wage. We know that inequality ha s grown, and it continue s to grow. But we
in New Zealand First understand the dignity  in doing an honest day’s work, and we
recognise too that an honest day’s work re quires an honest day’s pay. It is time for the
House to act. We need to vote this bill to the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee so that businesses and the people of New Zealand can actually have their
say.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: The Minimum Wage Amendment
Bill in the name of David Clark is, I am sure, a sincerely well-intentioned bill, but it is
flawed in its philosophy and its thrust and its focus. The way to create wealth for all
New Zealanders is to have strong, vibrant, growing businesses that can afford to pay
people well.
National does not support th is bill. We do support the hard-working people of New
Zealand, but not this bill. I do not want to endorse this bill, at all. Thank you.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is a real privilege and a pleasure to speak on the
Minimum Wage Amendment Bill. I want to congratulate my colleague David Clark on
his good work in bringing this bill to the House and his good fort une. In fact, he has
been so lucky with the members’ draw that I have invited him to come with me to the
races the next time I go. He has not actually taken that offer up yet, but I will forgive
him, because he has brought forward such  a good, solid Labour Party bill into this
House to reflect our policy of increasing th e minimum wage to $15 an hour. That is in
contrast to the platitudes that we get from the other side of the House. National
members want to say that they support ha rd-working, low-income people but will not
do anything to help them in their plight. Unlike that Government, the Labour Party is
prepared to take the practical steps that wi ll make a real difference for people in their
day-to-day lives. That is the difference between National and Labour.
I think it is really appropriate that we  are debating this bill on Women’s Suffrage
Day, because, again, this is a really practical  approach that we can take to support the
working women of this country. Sadly, what we do know, and this is according to the
5412 Minimum Wage Amendment Bill 19 Sep 2012
Department of Labour itself, is that 57.1 percent of females are on the minimum wage—
57.1 percent of women who are in paid empl oyment are, in fact, on the minimum wage.
So, if nothing else, this should tell us that if the Government is at all serious—at all
serious—about closing the gender pay gap, clearly increasing the minimum wage to $15
an hour would make a significant step in closing the gender pay gap in this country.
Women are far and away the largest de mographic group who are on the minimum
wage in New Zealand. They act ually outstrip 18 to 24-year-olds on the minimum wage.
There are 56.5 percent of 18 to 24-year-olds who are employed on the minimum wage.
But I want to pause and think about that just for a minute. What is it that the
Government feels comfortable with that women, no matter what age, end up staying on
the minimum wage in greater proportions than young people ente ring the employment
market for the first time? What is it about that that the Governme nt feels comfortable
with? Certainly on this side of the House we think that is wrong, and our view is shared
by Judy McGregor in her role as the E qual Employment Opportunities Commissioner.
Earlier this year she went undercover and did one of t hose minimum wage, low-paid
jobs in rest homes. She was horrified. In fact, she called it modern-day slavery. She
found that that very difficult work—physically  challenging, intell ectually challenging,
and mentally exhausting work—was largely being paid for on the minimum wage. And,
yes, it was almost all being delivered by women.
I want to challenge the Mi nister of Women’s Affairs about doing something about
that situation, because the only work that th e Ministry of Women’s Affairs is doing on
closing the gender pay gap is to say that a ll those rest home workers should go out and
get men’s jobs. That is the only work the mi nistry is doing to close the gender pay gap.
Apparently this would all be  fixed if only these women wo uld go out and be plumbers,
if only these women would go out and be el ectricians, if only these women would go
into those fields, because then we could so lve the gender pay gap. Well, I want to know
who will be looking after us in our old age, in rest homes. Who will be doing that work?
I do not want them doing it on the minimum wage.
One of the reasons why the Government has tried to pretend that it will not support
working families in this way, by increasing the minimum wage to $15 an hour, is that it
says that will drive more unemployment. I challenge those members to go and talk to
the miners in Huntly and tell them that that  is the reason why they are losing their jobs.
Those miners are not on the minimum wage, yet 120 of them in that small Waikato
town are losing their jobs because of that Government’s policies. That Government is
selling State-owned enterprises in that to wn, and that is making a huge difference to
unemployment—it is increasing it significantly  in the Waikato town of Huntly. So the
crocodile tears, the lack of policy, the lack of understanding, and the lack of compassion
from the National Government with regard to this bill do not make sense, and every
New Zealander knows it. I am very proud to recommend this bill to the House.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): I just want to ac knowledge that this
bill, the Minimum Wage Amendment Bill, is about the minimum wage, and I think it is
probably important to give a minimum time for my speech. I think one thing we need to
look at in this is th at changing the minimum wage in this fashion is arbitrary, but one
other aspect to consider is that when we talk about redistribution, we normally do that,
generally, through such things as welfare, ta xes, and so forth. What we have here is
placing a large burden on a group of taxpayers, being small businesses. It is not the right
way to do it. We cannot support this bill.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: The Minimum Wage
Amendment Bill is a chance to make a mu ch-needed step towards addressing child
poverty in New Zealand. The Children’s Commissioner’s report on child poverty makes
19 Sep 2012 Minimum Wage Amendment Bill 5413
for some distressing reading. Far too many of our children are growing up in households
that cannot make ends meet, let alone give them the best start in life.
I want to just comment brie fly on some of the hogwash that has been spoken from
the other side of the House through this de bate. There has been a lot of talk about
employment effects of raising the minimum wage by this small amount. That is absolute
rubbish—absolute rubbish. Research from the Department of Labour, the Government’s
own officials, has suggested that the minimu m wage rises that this Government has put
in have had no measurable effect on unemployment. That is very similar to the evidence
that comes through from Australia and from th e United Kingdom. It is absolutely true
that there is very little effect on employment , if any at all. Treasury says that on the
balance of probability, this will not have any effect on unemployment. As we know,
during the 1990s, when National put up the minimum wage—
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: When I was so rudely interru pted by the dinner break, I was
just making the very point that when Nationa l put up the minimum wage just 70c in the
9 years that it was in power in the 1990s, unemployment hovered up between 6 percent
and 11 percent. It never saw those levels ag ain under the Labour Government, when the
Labour Government put up the minimum wage  by a whole $5 over its 9 years. There
was more that needed to be done, but you cannot doubt that the minimum wage went
up, and what happened? Unemployment went down, down to the lowe st levels in the
Western World, so those who would argue that raising the minimum wage would cause
unemployment know themselves, deep down, th at they are wrong. They know they are
wrong.
What we also know is that even the m ean-spirited people opposite, those people who
would put a view like the one that Michael Woodhouse put, who have this mean view of
human nature that says that people do not want to get out and work, and you have to pay
them a whole lot of money to get them out and work, should understand that increasing
the minimum wage—even those who put th at mean-spirited view—would be a good
incentive to get people in work. But the reas on people want work and want to get out
there and work is that they care about their families. The jobs are not there, and there
are economic consequences to underp aying those people. There is the
underachievement of those young people who do not have full stomachs when they go
to school. They do not reach their potential. They do not become the future taxpaying
citizens whom we would wish them to beco me, because they have not reached their
potential. They get preventable illnesses through living in cold, damp, and overcrowded
conditions, from parents who do not have en ough money to look af ter them as they
would want to. Then there are the costs of antisocial behaviour.
We know very well that the economic case for opposing the minimum wage rise
does not stack up. The money that is paid in additional wages goes to stimulate the
economy. It also is true that small and medium enterprises largely already pay above the
minimum wage—certainly at a hi gher rate than other enterprises—and it actually levels
the playing field when their competitors are forced to raise the minimum wage also. So
that party opposite, I would say, is the en emy of small business. That party opposite
hates small business. It hates the fact that small business already pays decent wages and
is undercut by other operations that are on the lowest common denominator. We need to
pay a decent wage. We need to pay people the money that they need to live, to live good
lives, to reach their potential, and to cont ribute towards our economy. This Government
has the worst economic record in 50 year s. There are nearly  50,000 more people in
unemployment, and we know that 50,000 peopl e a year are leaving this country
permanently to go to Australia. The reason they  are going to Australia is that wages are
5414 Minimum Wage Amendment Bill 19 Sep 2012
higher there. Wages are higher there. Nearly NZ$20 is the ve ry lowest wage that gets
paid there. There is a huge gap between New Zealand and Australia in wages, and if we
continue to underpay, underpay, and unde rpay, we will see our children and
grandchildren disappearing off to Australia, where they can get paid better.
This bill is a chance to take a much-needed step towards addressing child poverty in
New Zealand. It is simple. It puts $60 a week  more in the wage packet of a 40-hour-a-
week worker so that they can put the nece ssities—the milk and cereal—out for the kids.
It is not a cure-all for child poverty, but it is a very good star t. I want to say in closing
that the Prime Minister has admitted that he could not live on the minimum wage. Why
does he think anyone else can? It is disgra ceful and shameful for the Government to
oppose this bill.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Minimum Wage Amendment
Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 59
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Part y 13; New Zealand First 8; M āori Party 3;
Mana 1.
Noes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.

OMBUDSMEN (COST RECOVERY) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Tēnā nō tātou katoa. I move, That the Ombudsmen
(Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate that this bill go to
the Government Administration Committee to enjoy consideration. This is a particularly
important piece of the machinery of our c onstitution and our Government, which has
been starved as a consequence of a very parsimonious approach taken by the current
Government to adequately resourcing the Office of the Ombudsmen. The Office of the
Ombudsmen has a bark that can have an effect not unlike a set of teeth marks on
recalcitrant bureaucrats. At all times we need to ensure that this office is suitably and
adequately resourced.
19 Sep 2012 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 5415
Unlike other members of the House, the officers of that office are not prone to florid,
extravagant language. It falls to me to be a moderate and sober representative for them
and their concerns, which were reflected in the select committee report that considered
the report of that office where no one on that side of the House stepped up to alleviate
the concerns, or certainly ade quately alleviate the concerns, of such figures as David
McGee QC and Dame Beverley Wakem, the two senior office holders in that institution
at the moment. They said that the workload is such that they are struggling to maintain
the quality of work and the quantity of output that has defined their work to date.
It is evident that their st aff are experiencing an enormous amount of work and their
staff are stretched. We, as members of Parliame nt, ought at all times to  ensure that they
are suitably resourced, because when their work is carried out on a consistent basis it
has the effect of ensuring that the bureaucr acy operates to a high standard of quality. I
have only to think, in the spirit of openness,  about the Zaoui debacle where Mel Smith,
the Ombudsman of that time, was able to de lve into the innards of the immigration
department, and indeed found that an indi vidual—I recall the name being Ian Smith—
had not only failed to provide the necessary information but al so failed in his duties. It
ended up costing the reputation of that department and, indeed, unnecessary amounts of
money. This is an example of why the office ought to be adequately funded.
Let me talk about what this bill, pithy in size, but deep, deep, deep in reach, seeks to
do. What this bill seeks to do is to estab lish a regime where reca lcitrant, uninterested,
indifferent bureaucrats have their department  face a financial cost should they not be
efficient and respond with alacrity to the co nstitutional concerns of the Office of the
Ombudsmen.
I need to say it may be said that by en abling the Office of the Ombudsmen to pass
on a charge as a consequence of the sluggish  behaviour of these bureaucrats, it could
give rise to a difficulty with a conflict of interest percep tion. That is not—that is not—
the case in terms of the thinking behind this bill and neither is it the case in the words
used in this bill. It is an opportunity for us to incentivise the Government departments
so that they realise that where their actions  do not measure up to th e expectations of the
Office of the Ombudsmen, then they do not get a free pass. But it is measuring the sense
of crisis—and I use that word because I am borrowing the language that was in the
actual report that quoted Dame Beverley as describing the paucity of resources reaching
a crisis level.
It may suit that side of the House to dimi nish the status of these officers of the
House. Indeed, they are about to do it to the environmental ombudsman. But on this
side we stand to ensure that such steps ca nnot be taken in a furtive way. They will be
publicised at all relevant points in this constitutional journey.
Why are we required to bring this bill, when  there is an opportunity on that side of
the House to simply increase the appropriation?  It might be said National is not doing
that because of the general scarcity of resour ces. But I go back to the central principle,
which Dame Beverley herself has pointed out . When her office is adequately resourced,
that actually enables it to resolve a whol e host of difficulties behind the scenes and
ensure that Government departments do not act in a fashion that worsens either the
reputation of the bureaucracy or further frus trates the legitimate interests and concerns
of New Zealanders when they seek out information.
All electors require a watchdog. This in stitution is a constitutionally mandated
watchdog, and the provenance of it goes back a little bit before my time. There could be
certain members of the House who remember Sir Guy Powles back in the 1960s—
slightly before my time—but that gives an  indication of how d eeply embedded this
institution is in our machinery of governme nt. And for what I woul d say is the miserly
sum of $700,000, which is the difference between the $300,000 gesture—which came
5416 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 19 Sep 2012
from the frugal, parsimonious, flinty Mr English, who seems to be diminishing the
status and the role of this organisation all for $700,000—and the additional million
dollars the office needs to get rid of th e backlog. We should be doing that. Why?
Because it is not reasonable for citizens to  wait incessantly because this institution, the
Office of the Ombudsmen, lacks the resources.
We have been told that nigh on 80 percen t of the complaints actually come from
individuals. There has been a host of col ourful complaints. Obvious ly, I think here not
only of the Zaoui case but of the work, for exam ple, that happened in the complaint that
was made in relation to the photos that the police had concerning the French rugby
player who got into a spot of bother. Th e Office of the Ombudsmen was available to
assist the media. Although that does not strike at the heart of the Government, it enables
the media—which from time to time can be rather irritating, but they have a role to play
as well; the fourth estate—to ensure that they get quality information.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Be nice to them.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Should I be nice to the medi a? Ninety-five percent, but
unfortunately words are inversely related to reality when you deal with the fourth estate.
That is another matter, and I wish them well in trying to ascertain what is really
happening with my Māori relations and their water hui and the Government.
But to come back, in terms of the Ombudsmen, I think it is important to bear in mind
that the office has jurisdiction over local government. It has jurisdiction over local
government, so its workload has grown, and it has probably grown on the back of the
global financial crisis, as people feel that  as the current Government is rationing
resources, their concerns are not being ade quately aired, they are not being adequately
considered, or, indeed, new grievances ar e growing. So why not ensure that the
watchdog, which is a force for good in relation to the electors, is adequately funded?
We realise that the refined voices of Dame  Beverley and Dave McGee will not take
on an acidic tone like those members of th e House—they will remain refined. But I
have only to quote the words of Dame Beverley  where she said that they are in crisis.
So it falls to us as parliamentarians to hi ghlight that sense of crisis, to warn both
ourselves and electors that if it is left to  wend its way unattended, mischief could be
afoot.
Thirdly, we as parliamentarians ought to ensure that the institutions that report to
Parliament are held in the highest public esteem. They are not asking for a great deal;
they are asking to be treated respectfully. I have got no doubt that the next report they
send in our direction will repeat the concerns that they suffer as a consequence of the
miserly level of the paucity of resources that they currently have access to. So this is a
legitimate piece of legislation—proposed le gislation. I look forward to it being—
perhaps forlornly—supported by all sentient members of the House and I would like to
put on record that, after the vote, they may prove to be a very diminished number.
Thank you very much.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I rise to speak on the Ombudsmen (Cost
Recovery) Amendment Bill put forward by the Hon Shane Jones. This bill would enable
the Ombudsmen to recover the cost of their investigations from the agencies being
investigated. This is the plan of the bill, but, frankly, it would not be the only outcome
and it would not, I do not think, be as effect ive as is suggested. This bill lacks the
thumbprint of work done by that member normally.
When I think back to the times I have work ed with the Hon Shane Jones, I think of
the Resource Management Act, and the em issions trading scheme—all sort of major
legislation that has involved him over the la st few years. Clearly he is a powerhouse
within the ranks of Labour, a towering intellect , and a powerful debater, yet this is what
we get. To put it flatly, this is a premature bill that will satisfy neither the needs of the
Office of the Ombudsmen nor the needs of the taxpayers of New Zealand. It is a bill that
seems to have been put together by someone simply wanting to fill the members’ bill
bucket. [Interruption] It is premature.
The Government acknowledges and appreciat es the importance of the oversight the
Ombudsmen provide and their co ntribution to a just and fa ir society. However, the
Government also acknowledges something th e member across the Chamber has yet to
and that has been the unintended fiscal cons equences that could arrive without proper
investigation of shif ting the costs from Government  agencies to the Ombudsmen’s
budget. It is a peculiar sugge stion and I really wonder how  involved Shane has been
with putting this bill together, because suddenly you are allowing people, you could say,
to write their own cheques.

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The promoter of this

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Sp eaker, and I acknowledge a
little bit of a lapse there in the normal—

items.text: An egregious lapse? I do not think it was an egregious
lapse, and I am grateful to the Rt Hon Winston Peters for just reminding me of that fact.
However, let us go back to the bill. Robe rt K Merton, then of Harvard University,
stated this in his article “The Unanticipate d Consequences of Purposive Social Action”.
It was published in the American Sociological Review . He quotes: “The most obvious
limitation to a correct anticipation of conseque nces of action is provided by the existing
state of knowledge.”
In this bill you are looking at half an equation. What you are saying is: “Gosh!
They’re a bit short of money. Let’s give them  the capacity to charge more.” I wonder
what sort of a political tool that could be in the hands of an  imaginative Opposition
member. It could be very, very useful. Ther e is no conflict of inte rest, we are assured.

quite common, when we stand to speak on a b ill, for members on the other side to say:
“Do you understand what you’re talking about?”; “Do you really know this bill?”. Well,
we can reverse the charge in  this case, and even though th e member used his wonderful
vocabulary, his entertaining tongue, his—

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on this Ombudsmen
(Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill. It is also  a pleasure to follow Mr Auchinvole, as it
always is. He is a member whom I could be charitable about and say that he usually has
good judgment, but in this case  he has misjudged the importa nce of this bill and the
impact that it will have. He has misjudged it.  He has talked about the other legislation
that the Hon Shane Jones has sh epherded through this House and the enormity of it. He
has said that this piece of legislation might be rats and mice—rats and mice—in
comparison with that legislation. But that s hows a complete lack of judgment from Mr
Auchinvole about the enormity and the importance of this bill.
The Office of the Ombudsmen does have a ve ry important constitutional function to
make sure that all our Government agencies ar e acting as to the laws that are passed in
this House, and their own inte rnal standards and processes. So to ensure that the Office
of the Ombudsmen is correctly  resourced is a very importa nt constitutional function of
this Government. To make su re that it is funded properly is also a very important
function of this Parliament and of the Government.
The Hon Shane Jones, the sponsor of this bi ll, said that the 2011 financial review of
the Office of the Ombudsmen said that the office was “in crisis”—in crisis—due to its
high caseload and its inability to meet its de mands. So this bill has travelled to this
stage, as a member’s bill, in order to try to rectify the issu e that was highlighted in that
2011 financial review, where it sa id the office was in crisis, and to make sure that the
office is properly resourced so it can carry out its very important constitutional
functions.
Those Government departments, those bur eaucrats that the Hon Shane Jones was
alluding to earlier on in his speech, have to be investigat ed properly when members of
the public, or maybe the media—the fourth estate—feel that they  have not had due
process followed. I know that as a former memb er of the fourth estate, when you got an
Official Information Act request declined and you did not feel that it had been processed
in a fair manner, then it was off to the Office of the Ombudsmen to try to make sure that
that information—which you thought you were rightfully trying to get your hands on—
was investigated as to whether the agency was acting in its correct capacity, according
to the legislation and its own internal pr ocesses. And I will be honest: some of the
Official Information Act requests, speaking as  a former journalist, asking for responses
from a Minister’s office were requests of th is party. But still, it is a very important
constitutional role that the Office of th e Ombudsmen has to make sure that those
Government agencies and Ministers’ offices  have followed the proper procedure as is
prescribed in law, and also in their own internal processes.
19 Sep 2012 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 5419
Just last week I had a constituent contact me who had come to the end of their tether
with a Government agency. They had spent a couple of years dealing with this agency.
They had felt they had come to the end of the process that they could with that agency,
which I will not name. The advice that I gave to that constituent was that the Office of
the Ombudsmen was the only fair and reasonab le place left for them to go. But I did
caution them that if they did decide to go dow n that road, it could be some considerable
time before they got a response. I say that out  of experience. On this side of the House
we know that we have put fo rward requests under the Offi cial Information Act, and
there have been attempts to—I think I will use a word that John Banks has used—
gerrymander the process in order to delay th e release of that information, or to not
release that information at all.
I think we need to make sure that th e Office of the Ombudsmen is resourced
properly. That is what this bill  tries to do in order for them  to recover some costs from
some of these agencies, so that very important  constitutional role of the Office of the
Ombudsmen can be carried out in order for the average Joe Citizen, for members of
Parliament, for agencies dealing with Gove rnment agencies, and, of course, for the
fourth estate to try to make sure that those legislative roles are adhered to.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am pleased to rise on be half of the Gr een Party to
support the Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Am endment Bill. Unlike many of the
speakers so far in this debate, with the ex ception of Mr Auchinvole,  I was part of the
Government Administration Committee that conducted the financial review into the
Office of the Ombudsmen that prompted the n eed for this legislat ion. I am pleased to
say that there can be no doubt that that offi ce is in crisis and that intervention is
required. I thought it would be helpful, first of  all, to reflect upon the importance of the
Office of the Ombudsmen in the vital—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I suspect I just saw
something that is thoroughly untoward in a democracy, particularly on a very important
matter, and that is the whip of a party going to tell other members not to take their call.
That is serious.
19 Sep 2012 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 5421

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That has got nothing to do with the order of the House.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I was reflecting on the vital role of the Ombudsmen and the
democratic and constitutional purpose that  they play. The Ombudsmen provide an
independent, impartial check on the quality, fa irness, and integrity of the administration
and decision making in the wider State sector . That includes investigating complaints
about the administrative conduct of centr al and local government agencies, and
complaints about the decisions  of Ministers of the Crow n; providing information and
guidance to employees wishing to repor t serious wrongdoing in their workplace,
including whistleblowing; and examining a nd monitoring the tr eatment of persons
detained in prisons, premises approved and agreed under the Immigration Act, health
and disability places of detention, and youth justice residences. We  often think of the
Ombudsmen in relation only to  the Official Information Act and complaints placed
about that, but, in fact, they have a far wi der role that also includes protecting and
monitoring the implementation of the UN Co nvention on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities. All of those func tions are very critical to both our constitution and our
democracy, and to the public’s right to hones ty, integrity, and transparency in those
processes. So it is a very important role indeed, and it is very important that it is an
office that is adequately resourced.
What we heard at the select committee duri ng the financial review that has prompted
this legislation is that the office is in  crisis. For example, the office’s budget is
established for a workload of 800 to 1,000 cases  at any given time, but it now routinely
deals with between 1,600 to 1,800 cases at any one time with no corresponding increase
in funding. At the time of the review the o ffice had 1,854 live cases, and of those over
300 were unassigned to an investigator. They  were sitting unassigned because all the
investigators were at their maximum tole rable workload—“tolerable” being a very
important word there. These are people who are under a great deal of stress in this
office. That meant that the office was consis tently failing to meet deadlines and it was
predicted that it would continue to do so b ecause of the lack of resources. The effect on
staff well-being in the office, we heard at  the committee, was very serious indeed.
Because it was currently understaffed by four investigators, and there had been no
movement in staff salaries since 2007, it had a very high staff turnover, and it also had
issues of staff sickness and stress leave becau se of high rates of serious illness and the
stresses placed on staff working under the c onditions that we have described, with the
growing complexity and volume of cases and th e lack of funding to deal with them. So
it is not a pretty picture to be a staff me mber in the Office of the Ombudsmen at the
moment. This bill from the H on Shane Jones helps, I think, to partially resolve these
issues by allowing the Ombudsme n the ability to recover cost s, as well as promoting
greater compliance from the Government departments and agencies being investigated.
If I may at this point give a personal example, I have a complaint with the
Ombudsman that has now been sitting undealt w ith for almost a year. I do not hold any
animus to the Office of the Ombudsmen for that state of affairs, but it is an important
case where the police, a Government agency, cited a legal opinion in the media to say
that they had decided to stop having sni ffer dogs doing drug test s in schools because
they had had a legal opinion telling them  that they should no longer do that. We
requested that legal opinion under the Official Information Act. It was not forthcoming,
so we made a complaint to the Ombudsman. It  transpired that no such legal opinion
actually existed, yet the agency—the police—had gone on record publicly claiming that
this opinion was the reason for no longer doing something. In fact, it did not exist. The
Ombudsmen should be able to give a remedy in this case, and because they are under-
resourced they are not able to  do so. That is one example of  why we need this bill. I
commend this bill to the House.
5422 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 19 Sep 2012

DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : I would like to begin by congratulating Shane
Jones on bringing this bill, the Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amen dment Bill, to the
House, because it is a co mmon-sense bill. People out there in the community know
common sense when they see it. Obviously, that does not include members on the other
side of the House, but it does include the va st majority of New Zealanders. They will
see it as a common-sense bill because it has three major advantages. First of all, it adds
a new income stream to the Office of the Ombudsmen to help meet demand, and we all
know that that demand is not being met currently. Why would anyone wish to stop that?
You would have to have no common sense at a ll. Some of those members over there, of
course, fall into that category. The bi ll will suppress demand, when Government
agencies realise that they need to avoid th e Ombudsman, because, with this legislation,
there would be associated costs. So it will help to suppress demand, and that is
something that common sense also dictates. Thirdly, it will mean that agencies are more
willing to satisfy applicants for official information without having to go to the
Ombudsman, and that is the way it should be to o. That is a third common-sense reason
that the members on the other side of the House will not be able to grasp, but the people
out there in the community will.
Like many other members here I have so me personal experience in dealing with
Government agencies and city councils and trying to get ba sic information out of them.
The fact that there is legislation that says they must actually do this in practice is not
enough. I would like to give you this example. Af ter my 15 years with the city council,
where I did a lot of work to assist the devel opment of recycling, I, with some others, set
up a company that would do commercial and industrial recycling—something that had
never been done properly in New Zealand before. In order to do that I needed the
cooperation of the Christchurch  City Council. I particularly  needed some information
from it. The council’s obstruction was abso lutely disgraceful. Y ou would have thought
that a city council would fall over backwards to help people who were trying to promote
commercial and industrial recycling in this country, but, no, the council’s imperatives
were that it wanted to protect its own opera tions, so it would not gi ve that information.
Replies to requests that were designed to  avoid giving important parts of the
19 Sep 2012 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 5423
information were what I got. There were  spurious reasons for not supplying the
information. There was a legalistic approach by  that particular agency to defer further
applications, using legal gobbledegook that meant nothing but created delay. There was
obvious obfuscation. There was a need for repeated applicatio ns to get basic
information that should have been voluntee red in the first place. The release of self-
serving versions of information with the use of large sections of blanking out of
documents was also employed by that city council, and is commonly employed by other
agencies and councils as well.
In addition to that there were, and are,  often deliberate delays beyond statutory
limits, because councils and agencies know they  can get away with it, and they should
not. Mostly, the expectation that failing to assist people with valid applications for
information will result only in an appeal to the Ombudsman, with no cost or other
serious ramifications, is what we see on a da ily basis with applications for official
information in this country. This bill will help  to change that. It will provide guidelines
regarding the amount of the costs and guidelines about the circumstances—so there you
have the safeguards.
The bill does extend to local government, and so it should. When you look at the
behaviour of the Christchurch City Counc il, which I am now deeply ashamed of, you
will see that this bill is absolutely necessary  to create some balance in the situation.
Councils and agencies can charge for information. Here we get something back in the
other direction—some balance in  the situation—where they w ill be charged if they do
not do what they should have done in the first place.
So for all those reasons—for all those reas ons—this bill deserves the support of this
House, and the House should do so with enthus iasm. I am deeply di sappointed that the
National members obviously do not care about the seriousne ss of this problem. Their
lack of common sense—

items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on a bill from the Hon
Shane Jones. The Ombudsmen (Cost Reco very) Amendment Bill is about an
organisation that probably is one of the most respected organisations in the State system
in New Zealand, so I want to acknowledge  the work of the Ombudsmen, all of them,
and their staff. I have been involved with them, I have seen them operate from the many
different positions I have held, and I certainly want to acknowledge their diligence and
the timeliness of the work they do. It is one of the most trusted organisations and
certainly one whose assistance is often called for when a citizen is at the end of their
tether, whoever that citizen may be. So I want to acknowledge that.
The second point I want to make is that, re ally, there is a wonderful elegance in the
primary proposal in this bill. It actually  will force a discipline amongst Government

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Indeed—I agree with the member . I must admit that I said to

departments, if this bill passes, to not only internalise their discipline about timely
response but also not subject themselves to  complaints that can be upheld. There are

with all of the might of these huge department s and all of the resources they produce, to
prevaricate, to take their time, and to really disable citizens from accessing their primary
right to information, citizens need redress from what is the ultimate public servant,
which is the Ombudsman. That is what the Ombudsman is—the ultimate public servant;
a servant of the public. They have internalised that.
So, here, what this bill is saying is th at if a complaint is made against you and
charges are involved—and, of course, the b ill also says the Office of the Ombudsmen
will set guidelines as to how this is to operate—then be warned that the costs incurred
will fall on you. They will fall on the departme nt; never on you, Mr Speaker. I would
never impugn you like that, at all. But that will breed a discipline.

social development, social welfare, and benef it reform work that th ey have been doing,

members opposite have not applied their minds to the elegant simplicity of this bill—

interested in dealing with these genuine c oncerns about the adequacy of the resource
base. They might think that this is a way of  better conserving resources, but you cannot
run the institutions that report to Parliament as some sorts of narrow, commercial, partly
privatised entities. They ar e organs of democracy, and th eir costs cannot be measured
purely in a day-to-day, year-t o-year monetary form. Their costs should be associated
with the value that the institution genera tes by improving people’ s confidence in the
behaviour of the executive.
So I want to remind that side of the House—just to show I am willing to talk about
mistakes that happened in an earlier ad ministration—that a former Ombudsman, Mr
Belgrave, looked into what was perhaps one of the nastiest incidents that I watched
befall a family as a consequence of lapses of professionalism and diligence from the
bureaucracy. I am thinking here of the young 17-year-old Liam Ashley, who suffered
the worst possible fate. It took the Ombudsmen to intrude and to investigate that. Those
are the sorts of cases we should not shy away from funding. I then go on to an example
that I might describe as an unwanted intr usion, where the Ombudsmen decided to have
a go at quantifying, or getting our side of the House, when we held the benches of
Treasury, to quantify the costs of that brilliant policy othe rwise known as interest-free
loans.
Both sides of the House from time to time will govern. Both sides of the House
realise that the advisers they trust in th e recesses of the bureaucracy do not always
deliver goods that enable us to  shine in the best fashion in  the House. They should be
held accountable for their actions, and that  is why the Office of the Ombudsmen ought
to be adequately funded. This is a device that enables them—not unlike Crown Law, not
unlike the Audit Office, which I unfortunately know a bit about at the moment, but that
is another matter. Both of those have the ability to recover costs, and what I am
promoting in this bill is a modest contribution that will enable this august institution to
cause the bureaucracy—where it is evident it has been sluggish, and it has not complied
with the law, or it has been, as Mel Smith said, so circuitous that it appears to have
broken the law.
19 Sep 2012 Ombudsmen (Cost Recovery) Amendment Bill 5427
That is why I am promoting this particular bill. It is not designed to create a problem
with conflict of interest perceptions. It is an avenue to improve the financial robustness
of the office, and I am very disappointed to he ar from that side of  the House that they
have taken such a short-term, superficial, very shallow sort of an approach. But such
shallowness, I accept, on this particular day has extended into this very well-thought-out
and well-conceived piece of legislation, because  it is shallowness that has characterised
question time today. But I will continue, as is my duty as a parliamentarian, to promote
this bill to the House.
